items.summary: You turn Release 2 into a work breakdown structure tied to the schedule and the register, find the critical path and float that decide whether the Release 2 acceptance gate holds on 2026-11-26, and estimate the riskiest task with three-point and PERT estimates.

read.heading: What the Release 2 WBS must hold
read.body:
Release 2 (clinician identity and access) covers role-based access control (RBAC), joiner-mover-leaver events from human resources (HR), multi-factor authentication (MFA) and single sign-on, privileged access, segregation of duties (SoD) and access reviews. A work breakdown structure (WBS) breaks that scope into deliverables, then into work packages small enough to estimate, assign and accept.

The 100% rule says the WBS holds all of the work in scope and nothing outside it, and every work package has one accountable owner, an acceptance test and a budget. Line up two sources, schedule tasks 13 to 20 in khn_schedule.csv and work packages WP-106 to WP-110 in khn_programme_register.csv, so every task and every dollar lands in exactly one work package.

| WBS | Deliverable | Schedule task | Register | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2.1 | Role catalogue and RBAC model | 13 | WP-106 | Daniel Osei (E-004) |
| 2.2 | Joiner-mover-leaver integration with HR | 14 | WP-107 | Nora Lindqvist (E-018) |
| 2.3 | MFA and single sign-on | 15 | WP-108 | none recorded |
| 2.4 | Privileged access and SoD controls | 16 | WP-109 | Daniel Osei (E-004) |
| 2.5 | Access-request value stream, third-quarter (Q3) access review and pilot | 17, 18, 19 | WP-110 | Grace Liu (E-005) |

Two findings fall out at once. WP-108 has no owner in the register, so nobody answers for its CAD 130,000 (Canadian dollars) until the sponsor names one (the finished baseline proposes Ahmed Haddad, E-017). And WP-110's dates (2026-11-09 to 2026-11-26) cover tasks 17, 18 and 19, so the pilot is funded inside it. The gate, task 20, is a zero-day milestone with no work of its own.

The WBS dictionary gives each line its description, owner, acceptance criteria, schedule task, budget and assumptions. The scope statement, WBS and WBS dictionary together form the scope baseline that later change requests are measured against.

read.heading: Sequence the work and know why each link exists
read.body:
Every link in khn_schedule.csv is finish-to-start with no lag: the successor cannot start until its predecessor finishes. Start-to-start, finish-to-finish, start-to-finish, leads and lags exist, but Beacon does not use them. The reason behind each link decides whether you can change it:
- Mandatory (hard logic): task 17 redesigns the access-request value stream after HR events flow (task 14), because the new stream is built on those events.
- Discretionary (preferred logic): task 18, the third-quarter (Q3) access review, waits for MFA (15) and privileged controls (16) so the review covers the new state. A team could choose otherwise, which makes this link a candidate for fast tracking.
- External: task 14 needs a feed from the HR and Payroll System (A-015), which the programme does not control.
- Internal: tasks 14, 15 and 16 wait for the Release 1 go-live gate (task 12) so the same people are not split across two releases.

The Release 2 network reads: 12 leads to 14, 15 and 16. Task 13 waits only for the threat model (task 7) and leads to 14 and 16. Task 14 leads to 17; 15 and 16 lead to 18; 17 and 18 lead to 19; 19 leads to the gate, task 20.

read.heading: Find the critical path with a forward and backward pass
read.body:
The critical path method (CPM) makes two passes through the network. The forward pass sets each task's early start to the latest early finish of its predecessors, then adds the duration to get the early finish. The backward pass starts from the finish date and works back to each task's late finish and late start. Total float is late start minus early start. The approved figures for Release 2, on a Monday to Friday calendar:

| ID | Task | Days | Early start | Early finish | Total float |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 13 | Design role catalogue and RBAC model | 12 | 2026-09-18 | 2026-10-05 | 14 |
| 14 | Integrate joiner-mover-leaver events from HR | 12 | 2026-10-26 | 2026-11-10 | 0 |
| 15 | Roll out MFA and single sign-on | 10 | 2026-10-26 | 2026-11-06 | 4 |
| 16 | Implement privileged access and SoD controls | 8 | 2026-10-26 | 2026-11-04 | 6 |
| 17 | Redesign the access-request value stream | 8 | 2026-11-11 | 2026-11-20 | 0 |
| 18 | Run Q3 access review and recertification | 6 | 2026-11-09 | 2026-11-16 | 4 |
| 19 | Release 2 pilot and acceptance testing | 4 | 2026-11-23 | 2026-11-26 | 0 |

The Release 2 critical path is 12 > 14 > 17 > 19 > 20: 12 + 8 + 4 = 24 working days from Monday 2026-10-26 to the gate on Thursday 2026-11-26, with zero float. It is one stretch of the programme critical path: 2 > 3 > 4 > 6 > 8 > 9 > 11 > 12 > 14 > 17 > 19 > 20 > 21 > 22 > 26 > 27 > 28.

Compare the parallel path 15 > 18 > 19: 10 + 6 + 4 = 20 days. That four-day gap is exactly why tasks 15 and 18 carry 4 days of float.

read.heading: Total float, free float and the calendar
read.body:
Total float is how far a task can slip before the finish date moves. Free float is how far it can slip before any successor's early start moves.

Task 16 shows the difference: total float 6, free float 2. It finishes on 2026-11-04, but task 18 cannot start until task 15 finishes on 2026-11-06, so task 16 can slip 2 days without anyone noticing. Slip it further and task 18 starts late, using up task 18's own float, although the gate holds until the slip passes 6 days. Task 15 has total float 4 but free float 0, so any slip delays task 18 at once.

Task 13 shares the largest float in the programme, 14 days, with task 7. It could start on 2026-09-18 and is not needed until 2026-10-23. That is good news for WP-106, which on 2026-10-01 was 40% complete against 75% planned.

The calendar is a hidden assumption. Beacon's schedule uses Monday to Friday with no holidays. Remembrance Day, Wednesday 2026-11-11, is the very day critical task 17 is due to start. Add it as a non-working day and a forward pass moves task 17 to 2026-11-12 through 2026-11-23, the Release 2 gate to Friday 2026-11-27 and programme acceptance to 2026-12-18. Thanksgiving (Monday 2026-10-12) falls inside critical Release 1 task 8. Add both holidays and the Release 1 gate moves to Monday 2026-10-26, the Release 2 gate to Monday 2026-11-30 and programme acceptance to Monday 2026-12-21. Decide on holidays before you baseline: Beacon's finished baseline keeps 2026-11-26, logs the holiday as a risk and agrees a response in advance.

read.heading: Estimate durations: analogous, parametric, three-point and PERT
read.body:
Four ways to estimate a duration:
- Analogous (top-down): adjust a similar past piece of work. Example (estimate): an earlier HR-feed integration took about 10 days; adding agency and vendor end dates makes 12 for task 14.
- Parametric: a unit rate times a quantity. Example (estimate): 11 roles in use in khn_identity.csv at about 1 day each, plus 1 day for approval, gives 12 days for task 13.
- Bottom-up: estimate each activity and add them up. Most accurate, slowest.
- Three-point: ask for optimistic (O), most likely (M) and pessimistic (P) values. The triangular mean is (O + M + P) / 3. PERT (Program Evaluation and Review Technique, a beta distribution) weights the most likely value: (O + 4M + P) / 6. The standard deviation is about (P - O) / 6.

Worked example for task 14, using the task owners' estimates of 2026-10-07 (estimates, not data): O = 10, M = 11, P = 18 days.
- Triangular: (10 + 11 + 18) / 3 = 13.0 days.
- PERT: (10 + 44 + 18) / 6 = 12.0 days.
- Standard deviation: (18 - 10) / 6 = 1.33 days. Under the usual normal approximation, roughly 68% of outcomes fall within one standard deviation (about 10.7 to 13.3 days) and about 95% within two (about 9.3 to 14.7 days).

The schedule holds 12 days for task 14, exactly the PERT value, so there is no slack inside the estimate. Do the same for the other critical tasks (task 17 from 6, 7 and 14 days gives 8.0; task 19 from 3, 4 and 5 gives 4.0) and the expected critical path is 12 + 8 + 4 = 24 days, exactly the 24 available. To combine tasks, add variances (standard deviation squared), not standard deviations: 1.78 + 1.78 + 0.11 = 3.67, and its square root gives a path standard deviation of about 1.9 days. An expected finish equal to the gate means only about a 50% chance of holding it. That is a reason to agree a response in advance, such as fast tracking task 17 if task 14 slips by more than a day, not a reason to change the numbers quietly.

read.heading: Compress if you must, then set the baseline
read.body:
If the gate is at risk, there are two classic compression techniques:
- Crashing adds resources to critical tasks to shorten them. It costs money and only helps on the critical path. Putting a second systems administrator on task 14 is crashing.
- Fast tracking runs in parallel tasks that were planned in sequence. It costs nothing up front but raises risk and rework. Starting task 17's value-stream workshops while task 14 is still in testing is fast tracking.

Shortening a task that has float, such as task 15, buys nothing at the gate. Always check the path before you spend.

When the sponsor approves the schedule, save it as the schedule baseline (in Microsoft Project, Project tab, Set Baseline) and record version, date and approver. From then on you report variance against it and change it only through change control.

keyTerms.term: Work breakdown structure (WBS) and the 100% rule
keyTerms.definition: A deliverable-based breakdown of the total scope into work packages; the 100% rule says it contains all of the work in scope and nothing outside it.
The lowest level of the WBS, small enough to estimate, schedule, assign to one accountable owner and accept, such as WP-107 Joiner-mover-leaver integration with HR.
The longest path through the schedule network; its tasks have zero total float, so any slip moves the finish. For Release 2 it is 12 > 14 > 17 > 19 > 20.
How many working days a task can slip before the project finish moves; late start minus early start. Task 13 has 14 days, the most in Beacon (tied with task 7).
How many working days a task can slip before its successor's early start moves. Task 16 has 6 days of total float but only 2 of free float.
A three-point weighted estimate, (O + 4M + P) / 6, with standard deviation about (P - O) / 6. Estimates of 10, 11 and 18 days give 12.0 and 1.33.
Shortening critical-path tasks by adding resources, which raises cost and only helps when applied to tasks on the critical path.
Overlapping critical tasks that were planned in sequence; it saves time without new cost but increases the risk of rework.

build.goal: Produce the schedule half of the Release 2 schedule and cost baseline: a Release 2 WBS tied to tasks 13 to 20 and WP-106 to WP-110, the critical path and float, a three-point estimate for task 14, and a calendar decision for the sponsor.
steps: In Project, open Release 2 and the document Release 2 schedule and cost baseline. Read How to write it, then start the WBS section in the writing area.
Write the five WBS lines (2.1 to 2.5) with schedule task, register work package and owner, and record that WP-108 has no owner and that WP-110 funds tasks 17, 18 and 19.
From Practice, Labs, take khn_schedule.csv. In Microsoft Project set the project start to 2026-09-01, import the file, indent rows 2 to 28 under row 1, and check that task 20 lands on 2026-11-26.
Turn on Critical Tasks and add the Total Slack and Free Slack columns. Record the Release 2 critical path (12 > 14 > 17 > 19 > 20) and the float of tasks 13, 15, 16 and 18 in the document.

Collect optimistic, most likely and pessimistic durations for tasks 14 to 19 from the task owners, label them as estimates, and write each PERT value, the critical-path standard deviation, the chance of holding the gate and the response you propose.
In a copy of the plan, add 2026-11-11 and then 2026-10-12 as non-working days with Change Working Time, record the new gate dates, and write the calendar decision you will ask the sponsor to make.
Note that the schedule baseline is set only after approval, with version, date and approver, then compare your document with See the finished example.
build.modelAnswer: Release 2 critical path: 12 Release 1 go-live gate (2026-10-23) > 14 Integrate joiner-mover-leaver events from HR (12d, 2026-10-26 to 2026-11-10) > 17 Redesign the access-request value stream (8d, to 2026-11-20) > 19 Pilot and acceptance testing (4d, to 2026-11-26) > 20 gate. 24 working days, zero float. Float: task 13 has 14 days, 16 has 6 (free 2), 15 and 18 have 4. Task 14 PERT from estimates 10/11/18 is 12.0 days (SD 1.33). The expected critical path is 24 days with an SD of about 1.9, so the gate has about a 50% chance: agreed response, fast-track task 17 if task 14 slips more than 1 day. Remembrance Day as a holiday moves the gate to 2026-11-27, and with Thanksgiving as well to 2026-11-30; the baseline keeps 2026-11-26 and logs the risk.

examTips.tip: Process task 8, Plan and manage schedule: when a task slips, compare the slip with its total float. Task 16 can slip 6 days before the Release 2 gate moves, but only 2 days before task 18 is affected (its free float).

Read whether a three-point question wants the triangular mean or PERT. With 10, 11 and 18 days the answers differ: 13.0 versus 12.0. The standard deviation exam questions expect is (P - O) / 6, here 1.33.

Crashing adds cost; fast tracking adds risk. If the scenario says the budget is fixed, fast tracking is usually the better first answer; if rework would be dangerous, crash. Either one helps only on the critical path.

pitfalls: Shortening a task that has float, such as task 15 with 4 days. Only critical tasks move the gate, so compress 14, 17 or 19.
Treating the calendar as neutral. Remembrance Day on 2026-11-11 sits on the early start of critical task 17; decide on holidays before approval.
Building the WBS from the schedule alone. Every task and every dollar must land in one work package, and WP-108 still has no owner.
Changing a duration quietly because a new estimate differs from the plan. Estimates inform reserve and response decisions; the baseline changes only with approval.

check.q: Task 15 (Roll out MFA and single sign-on) slips by 3 working days. Does the Release 2 gate move, and what else is affected?
check.a: No. Task 15 has 4 days of total float, so the gate on 2026-11-26 holds. Its free float is 0, so task 18 (the Q3 access review) starts 3 days late, and the path 15 > 18 > 19 is left with only 1 day of float.

check.q: Using estimates O = 10, M = 11 and P = 18 days for task 14, what are the PERT estimate and standard deviation, and what do they mean for the gate?
check.a: PERT = (10 + 4 x 11 + 18) / 6 = 12.0 days; standard deviation = (18 - 10) / 6 = 1.33 days. That equals the 12 days planned, so there is no buffer. Along the critical path (14, 17, 19) the expected total is 24 days, exactly the time available, with a path standard deviation of about 1.9 days, so the gate has only about a 50% chance. Agree a response before the baseline, such as fast tracking task 17 if task 14 slips more than a day.

check.q: Why does task 13 have 14 days of total float when it belongs to Release 2?
check.a: It depends only on task 7, so it can run from 2026-09-18 to 2026-10-05, but its successors (14 and 16) cannot start until after the Release 1 go-live gate on 2026-10-23. Its late finish is therefore 2026-10-23, which gives 14 working days of float. That is why WP-106 being behind plan on 2026-10-01 does not yet threaten the gate.

items.summary: You estimate Release 2 cost and resources, fix the over-allocations the schedule hides, separate contingency from the CAD 120,000 management reserve, baseline Release 2's CAD 460,000 as a time-phased cost baseline, and record a tailored delivery approach.

read.heading: Start from the cleaned register
read.body:
Your cost baseline starts from khn_programme_register.csv after the Kestrel cleaning rules. For Release 2 that leaves five work packages:

| Work package | Budget (CAD) | Planned dates | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| WP-106 Role catalogue and RBAC design | 90,000 | 2026-09-18 to 2026-10-05 | E-004 |
| WP-107 Joiner-mover-leaver integration with HR | 110,000 | 2026-10-26 to 2026-11-10 | E-018 |
| WP-108 MFA and single sign-on rollout | 130,000 | 2026-10-26 to 2026-11-06 | missing |
| WP-109 Privileged access and segregation of duties | 70,000 | 2026-10-26 to 2026-11-04 | E-004 |
| WP-110 Access-request value stream and access reviews | 60,000 | 2026-11-09 to 2026-11-26 | E-005 |

Here RBAC is role-based access control, HR is human resources and MFA is multi-factor authentication. The total is the Release 2 budget at completion (BAC): CAD 460,000 (Canadian dollars), part of the programme BAC of CAD 1,200,000.

Two repairs come before any baseline. WP-109's planned finish in the file is 2026-11-31, a date that does not exist; the authoritative source, task 16 in the schedule, finishes on 2026-11-04. WP-108 has no owner, and a budget nobody answers for is not ready to baseline, so ask the sponsor, Dr. Helen Marchetti (E-001), to name one. Watch for the two wrong programme totals too: CAD 1,220,000 if you add every row, and CAD 1,080,000 if you remove the duplicate but leave WP-113's sign error.

read.heading: Estimate cost three ways
read.body:
The methods you used for duration work for cost too. Each has its place:
- Analogous: scale the cost of similar past work. Fast, cheap, and only as good as the similarity. Release 1 is a warning analogue: on 2026-10-01 its cost performance index (CPI) was 0.89, so each dollar spent earned 89 cents of planned work. If Release 2 runs the same way, expect it to cost more than planned unless something changes.
- Parametric: a rate times a quantity. Example (an assumed internal rate, not Kestrel data): systems administrator time on task 14 is 12 days x 7.5 hours x CAD 95 per hour = CAD 8,550.
- Bottom-up: estimate each activity and roll the totals up to the work package. Slower, and the most defensible when a sponsor challenges a number.
- Three-point: the same O, M and P logic. Example for the WP-108 work (estimates): optimistic CAD 100,000, most likely 108,000, pessimistic 128,000. The PERT (Program Evaluation and Review Technique) weighted mean = (100,000 + 4 x 108,000 + 128,000) / 6 = CAD 110,000, with a standard deviation of about CAD 4,667. That is the work estimate in Beacon's finished baseline; the rest of WP-108's CAD 130,000 budget is CAD 20,000 of contingency for named risks.

Whatever the method, write down the basis of estimate: who estimated, the assumptions, the range and the confidence. An estimate without a basis cannot be defended or improved.

read.heading: Plan resources and fix the over-allocation
read.body:
The Resource Names column in khn_schedule.csv lists roles. Load them in Microsoft Project and the Resource Usage view shows two Release 2 problems:
- The Systems Administrator role is on tasks 14, 15 and 16, which all start on 2026-10-26. From 2026-10-26 to 2026-11-04 the role is booked on three tasks at once.
- The Service Desk Manager is on tasks 17 and 18, which overlap from 2026-11-11 to 2026-11-16, and then on task 19.

Two techniques resolve over-allocation:
- Resource smoothing moves non-critical work within its float, so the finish date stays put. In Project this is levelling with the option Level only within available slack. Task 16 has 6 days of float and task 15 has 4, but task 14 runs to 2026-11-10, so smoothing alone cannot free one administrator for all three tasks.
- Resource levelling moves work to fit the resources you have, even if the critical path and finish move. Levelling one administrator across tasks 14, 15 and 16 would push the gate.

The practical answer is to assign people, not roles. Do not give task 16 to Kevin Park (E-009): it removes his own conflicting rights (issue I-01). The finished baseline proposes Kevin Park with Nora Lindqvist (E-018) on task 14, Ahmed Haddad (E-017) on task 15 and Lucas Girard (E-033) on task 16, for Marcus Bell (E-002) to confirm. For the Service Desk Manager, Grace Liu leads both tasks 17 and 18 while they overlap and the Programme Manager chases review items that week; record that as an assumption.

read.heading: Contingency reserve versus management reserve
read.body:
- Contingency reserve covers identified risks, the known unknowns. It sits inside the cost baseline, is sized from the risk register, and the programme manager uses it under agreed rules when a named risk occurs.
- Management reserve covers unidentified risks, the unknown unknowns. It sits outside the cost baseline, is held by management, and using it needs a change request and sponsor approval. Earned value is never calculated on it.

Beacon's management reserve is CAD 120,000 (agreed), held by Dr. Helen Marchetti outside the register, so total authorized funding is CAD 1,320,000.

A simple way to size contingency is expected monetary value (EMV) = probability x impact. For R-03 (MFA prompts slow clinicians at shared workstations, owner Janelle Cardinal), the team judges a 40% chance (estimate) of extra support costing about CAD 30,000 (estimate): EMV = 0.4 x 30,000 = CAD 12,000. A late identity platform contract, at 25% x CAD 32,000, adds CAD 8,000, so WP-108 carries CAD 20,000 of contingency. Add the EMVs of the Release 2 risks you choose to fund and show the contingency as named lines inside the 460,000, so everyone can see what it protects. In Beacon's finished baseline the five work packages hold CAD 412,000 of work estimates and CAD 48,000 of contingency (estimates).

Now look at R-08. On 2026-10-01 the programme estimate at completion (EAC) was CAD 1,342,500 against a BAC of 1,200,000, a variance at completion of CAD -142,500. That is CAD 22,500 more than total authorized funding (1,342,500 - 1,320,000), so the whole reserve could not cover it. The reserve is not a cushion for poor cost performance; Marcus Bell (E-002), owner of R-08, needs corrective action as well.

read.heading: Build the time-phased cost baseline
read.body:
The cost baseline is the approved, time-phased budget, including contingency and excluding management reserve. Time-phased means you know how much should be spent by when, which is what planned value (PV) is later measured against.

Spreading each Release 2 work package evenly across its working days (an assumption; real spending is lumpier) gives:

| Month | Release 2 spend (CAD) | Cumulative (CAD) |
|---|---|---|
| September 2026 | 67,500 | 67,500 |
| October 2026 | 177,083 | 244,583 |
| November 2026 | 215,417 | 460,000 |

Plotted, the cumulative column is the S-curve. The finished baseline shows the same curve week by week, rounded to the nearest hundred (for example 244,600 by 2026-10-30). September is all WP-106: 9 of its 12 working days fall in September, which matches its planned 75% on 2026-10-01. At that date WP-106 had earned 40% and spent CAD 39,600, so Release 2 shows PV CAD 67,500, earned value (EV) CAD 36,000 and actual cost (AC) CAD 39,600 (computed from the register). Week 9 turns this into an earned value report.

Check one more thing now: funding. October and November carry the peaks because tasks 14, 15 and 16 run side by side. If Kestrel releases money by month, the funding limit must cover those months, or the schedule has to bend to the money.

read.heading: Choose and tailor the delivery approach
read.body:
- Predictive: scope, schedule and cost are planned up front and changed through control. It suits fixed dates, regulated work and well-understood scope.
- Agile (adaptive): short cycles, working increments, and a backlog the product owner reprioritizes from feedback. It suits work where the right answer emerges as people use it.
- Hybrid: a deliberate mix.

Beacon is hybrid. The programme has fixed gates (2026-11-26 for Release 2), one budget, one change-control board and privacy work that must finish before go-live, so the frame is predictive. Inside Release 2, two pieces gain from iteration: the role catalogue (show the matrix to nurses and clerks, refine, repeat) and the access-request redesign (pilot with one unit, measure, adjust).

Tailoring means choosing these on purpose and writing down why: risk, regulatory needs, how stable the requirements are, team size, and how often stakeholders can give feedback. A tailoring note in the baseline might read: predictive gates, baselines and change control; short iterations for the access-request redesign in WP-110, each reviewed by the task 19 pilot users; any change to scope, dates or budget still goes to the change-control board.

keyTerms.definition: The approved, time-phased budget for the work, including contingency reserve and excluding management reserve; for Release 2 it totals CAD 460,000.
Budget inside the cost baseline set aside for identified risks, sized from the risk register, for example by expected monetary value.
Budget outside the cost baseline for unidentified risks, held by the sponsor; Beacon's is CAD 120,000 and using it requires a change request.
Probability multiplied by impact for a risk; a 40% chance of a CAD 30,000 impact gives an EMV of CAD 12,000.
Moving non-critical work within its float to even out resource demand without changing the finish date or the critical path.
Rescheduling work to fit available resources, which can move the critical path and the finish date.
Deliberately choosing and adapting the delivery approach, processes and artifacts to fit the project's risk, regulation, team and stakeholders, and recording why.

examTips.tip: Process task 6, Plan and manage finance: the cost baseline includes contingency reserve but not management reserve, and the project budget is the cost baseline plus management reserve. Funding an unidentified risk that has occurred goes through a change request to use management reserve.

Process task 4, Plan and manage resources: resource smoothing stays within float and never moves the finish; resource levelling can move the critical path. If the scenario says the end date is fixed, smoothing is the expected answer.

Process task 1, Develop an integrated project management plan and plan delivery: in hybrid scenarios the strongest answer usually keeps governance and compliance predictive while letting uncertain work iterate, and records the tailoring decision.

pitfalls: Putting the CAD 120,000 management reserve into the cost baseline or the S-curve. It sits outside both, so planned value and earned value never include it.
Adding up the raw register: every row gives CAD 1,220,000 and removing only the duplicate gives 1,080,000. The approved BAC is 1,200,000, of which Release 2 is 460,000.
Treating a role as a person. Three tasks booked to Systems Administrator on 2026-10-26 look fine until you assign real names.
Calling reserve a buffer for overspending. Contingency is for named risks; a CPI of 0.89 needs corrective action, not just a reserve draw.

check.q: Your sponsor asks why the CAD 120,000 management reserve does not appear in the Release 2 S-curve. What do you say?
check.a: Management reserve is held by the sponsor for unidentified risks and sits outside the cost baseline. The S-curve is the time-phased cost baseline, so it shows only Release 2's CAD 460,000, including any contingency lines. Reserve money enters the baseline only when an approved change request releases it, and the baseline is then updated.

check.q: What over-allocation does the Release 2 schedule create, and how would you resolve it without moving the 2026-11-26 gate?
check.a: The Systems Administrator role is booked on tasks 14, 15 and 16 from 2026-10-26, and task 14 is critical until 2026-11-10, so smoothing within the float of task 15 (4 days) and task 16 (6 days) cannot free one person. Assign named administrators instead: one on critical task 14, and on task 16 an administrator who is not Kevin Park (E-009), because that task removes his conflicting rights. The finished baseline proposes Kevin Park on task 14, Ahmed Haddad (E-017) on task 15 and Lucas Girard (E-033) on task 16.

check.q: Using the register, what were Release 2's PV, EV and AC on 2026-10-01, and which work package explains them?

The other Release 2 work packages had not started. Task 13's 14 days of float mean the gate is not yet at risk, but the gap needs watching.

items.summary: You choose contract types for what Release 2 buys, set mandatory screens and weighted criteria to select a supplier, and write the security and privacy controls Kestrel needs from each vendor in khn_vendors.csv, from assurance reports to remote access and contract-end removal.

read.heading: What Release 2 has to buy or change
read.body:
Release 2 touches suppliers in two ways. First, Kestrel may need to acquire something new: identity platform capability for multi-factor authentication (MFA), single sign-on and privileged access management (PAM), plus implementation help. Second, three existing suppliers have people who hold Kestrel accounts: engineers from Meridian Clinical Systems (V-01), support staff from NorthArc Cloud (V-02) and agency nurses from ClearPath Staffing (V-03), whose starts and ends human resources (HR) records. Their contracts decide how fast Kestrel hears that someone has left.

Start each need with make-or-buy: can Kestrel's Identity Directory (A-007) do it, or must you buy? Then write a statement of work (SOW): what is delivered, to what standard, by when, and how it is accepted.

Pick the procurement document to match what you know:
- Request for information (RFI): you are still learning what suppliers can offer.
- Request for proposal (RFP): you need suppliers to propose a solution and a price.
- Request for quotation (RFQ): the item is defined and you only need a price.

For the identity platform an RFP fits: you know the outcome, fast phishing-resistant sign-in at shared workstations, but not the best way to reach it.

read.heading: Contract types and who carries the risk
read.body:
The contract type decides who pays when costs run over.

| Type | How the price works | Who carries cost risk | Use it when |
|---|---|---|---|
| Firm fixed price (FFP) | One agreed price for defined scope | Seller | Scope is clear and stable |
| Fixed price incentive fee (FPIF) | Fixed price plus an incentive for beating targets, up to a ceiling | Mostly seller, shared | Clear scope and you want performance |
| Fixed price with economic price adjustment (FP-EPA) | Fixed price adjusted by named indices such as inflation | Seller, with the adjustment shared | Contracts that run several years |
| Cost plus fixed fee (CPFF) | Allowable costs plus a fixed fee | Buyer | Scope is uncertain |
| Cost plus incentive fee (CPIF) | Costs plus a fee that moves with performance against targets | Buyer, shared | Uncertain scope, cost control wanted |
| Cost plus award fee (CPAF) | Costs plus a fee the buyer awards against its own criteria | Buyer | Performance is hard to measure |
| Time and materials (T&M) | Agreed rates for hours and materials | Buyer | Small or undefined work, extra staff |

Lumen Analytics Partners (V-05) has a fixed-price contract for Release 1: Lumen carried the cost risk, and work outside the agreed scope is a contract change. For Release 2 a sensible split (a proposal) is a fixed price for the defined MFA and single sign-on configuration, paid at accepted milestones, and time and materials with a not-to-exceed cap for the uncertain HR-feed integration.

read.heading: Select suppliers with screens and weighted scoring
read.body:
Set the source selection criteria before proposals arrive, in two layers.

1. Mandatory screens, pass or fail: Kestrel data held in Canada (a Kestrel contract requirement, not a law); an independent assurance report under 12 months old; breach notice to Kestrel within 24 hours (proposed); a right-to-audit clause; and MFA on the supplier's own administrator access. A proposal that fails a screen is out, however cheap.
2. Weighted scoring of what is left.

Worked example with illustrative panel scores (not Kestrel data), on a scale of 1 to 5:

| Criterion | Weight | Proposal A | Proposal B | Proposal C |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sign-in speed at shared clinical workstations (R-03) | 30% | 4 | 5 | 3 |
| Security and assurance | 25% | 5 | 3 | 4 |
| Fit with the Identity Directory (A-007) and Virtual Desktop Service (A-008) | 20% | 4 | 3 | 3 |
| Three-year cost | 15% | 3 | 5 | 4 |
| Ability to start on 2026-10-26 | 10% | 4 | 3 | 5 |
| Weighted total | 100% | 4.10 | 3.90 | 3.60 |

Proposal A wins narrowly. The weights, agreed by Marcus Bell, Daniel Osei and Janelle Cardinal, carry Kestrel's values: B is the fastest at the workstation and the cheapest, but its weaker security and integration scores cost it the lead. A close result means check the evidence behind the top scores before you sign. Record who scored, their evidence and any conflicts of interest.

read.heading: Supplier security and privacy controls
read.body:
Contracts are controls. Kestrel's clauses for any supplier touching its systems or data:
- Assurance: an independent SOC 2 (System and Organization Controls 2) Type II report, or an equivalent such as ISO/IEC 27001 certification, every year. Type I says controls were designed properly at a point in time; Type II says an auditor tested that they operated over a period. Read the exceptions and the complementary user entity controls, which Kestrel must run itself. A bridge letter covers the gap since the report period ended.
- Right to audit: Kestrel or its auditor may assess the supplier's controls, and the supplier must fix findings.
- Breach notification: the supplier tells Kestrel within 24 hours (proposed). Under the Health Information Act (HIA), section 60.1, an affiliate must tell the custodian, and the custodian must notify the Information and Privacy Commissioner, the Minister responsible under the Act and the affected individuals as soon as practicable where there is a risk of harm. A supplier's delay becomes Kestrel's delay.
- Data location: Kestrel's contract requirement keeps its data in Canada unless the Chief Privacy Officer approves an exception. No Alberta statute bans storage outside Canada; HIA section 60 requires safeguards for health information stored or used outside Alberta.
- Remote access: named accounts, MFA every time, sessions brokered through PAM and recorded, approval per session, accounts ended on the contract end date.
- People: contract workers serving Kestrel are affiliates under the HIA, so they follow Kestrel's privacy management program and Kestrel stays responsible for them.

read.heading: What khn_vendors.csv tells you
read.body:
| Vendor | Data location | Remote access | Last assurance | Contract end | Finding |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| V-01 Meridian Clinical Systems | Canada | Yes | 2026-03-31 | 2029-03-31 | E-015 Raj Patel: privileged, no MFA, no end date |
| V-02 NorthArc Cloud | Canada | Yes | 2026-05-15 | 2028-06-30 | E-039 keeps Backup Platform access under exception AR-010 |
| V-03 ClearPath Staffing | Canada | No | none | 2027-03-31 | No report; agency end dates do not reach Kestrel (E-014) |
| V-04 Sentinel SOC Services | United States | Yes | 2025-11-30 | 2027-12-31 | Data outside Canada: privacy review and safeguards (R-05) |
| V-05 Lumen Analytics Partners | Canada | Yes | 2025-06-30 | 2026-11-30 | Report over 12 months old; contract ends within 90 days (R-07) |

Four of the five have remote access. Match control to risk. ClearPath runs no Kestrel system and has no remote access, so a security questionnaire plus firm terms on end dates, training and named accounts fits. Sentinel, the managed security operations centre (SOC), is the opposite: security logs carry staff identities and, if Clinical Information System audit events are forwarded, patient identifiers. That makes R-05 a privacy question first, owned by Priya Raman (E-003): remove patient identifiers before export, require processing in Canada, or approve an exception with safeguards that meet section 60. Lumen needs a current report or bridge letter; its accounts end on 2026-11-30.

read.heading: Partners and suppliers in ITIL and CISSP
read.body:
ITIL's Partners and Suppliers dimension asks how other organizations help design, build, run and support a service, and how those relationships are governed. For the access service, ClearPath's start and end dates and Meridian's engineer roster are inputs to the value stream, not side issues. In the ITIL Version 5 lifecycle, the Acquire stage is where Kestrel obtains components from partners, and the contract terms above are part of what it acquires. ITIL's supplier management practice then keeps performance, risk and the relationship under review, for example in a quarterly meeting covering each supplier's accounts, incidents, assurance report and contract dates.

In CISSP terms this is supply chain risk management. You inherit your suppliers' weaknesses, so you assess them before the contract, bind them in it, monitor them during it, and remove their access at the end. Beacon's weakest supply-chain point today is two accounts, E-014 and E-015, that outlived or never had an end date.

keyTerms.definition: A contract with one agreed price for defined scope; the seller carries the cost risk, so scope changes become contract changes.
The buyer pays allowable costs plus a fee (fixed, incentive or award), so the buyer carries most of the cost risk; it suits uncertain scope.
Payment at agreed rates for hours and materials; the buyer carries the risk, which a not-to-exceed cap limits.
A selection method that multiplies each criterion's score by its weight and adds them, applied only after mandatory pass or fail screens.
An independent auditor's report on whether a service organization's controls were designed and operated over a period, not just at a point in time.
A contract clause letting the buyer or its auditor assess the supplier's controls and requiring the supplier to fix findings.
An individual or organization acting for a custodian, including employees and contractors; affiliates follow the custodian's privacy management program and the custodian stays responsible for them.

examTips.tip: Process task 5, Plan and manage procurement: match the contract type to scope certainty. Clear scope points to fixed price (seller risk); unclear scope to cost-reimbursable (buyer risk); small or urgent undefined work to time and materials, ideally capped.

Domain 1 Security and Risk Management (supply chain risk management): a SOC 2 Type II report tests operating effectiveness over a period, a Type I covers design at a point in time. For the strongest assurance before signing, Type II plus a right-to-audit clause beats a questionnaire.

Partners and Suppliers is one of the four dimensions. If a question describes agency end dates or vendor contracts shaping how a service works, that is this dimension, and obtaining those components belongs to the Acquire stage of the lifecycle.

pitfalls: Saying Alberta law forbids storing health information outside Canada. It does not; Kestrel's Canada rule is a contract requirement, and the Health Information Act requires safeguards for information stored or used outside Alberta.
Scoring proposals before applying mandatory screens. A cheap proposal that fails data location or assurance should never reach the scoring table.
Accepting an old assurance report. Lumen's is dated 2025-06-30, more than 12 months before 2026-10-01; ask for a current report or a bridge letter.
Forgetting that a contract end is an access event. Lumen's contract ends 2026-11-30, and its accounts must end the same day.

check.q: Why is time and materials with a not-to-exceed cap reasonable for the HR-feed integration but not for the defined MFA configuration?
check.a: The HR-feed effort is uncertain, so a fixed price would be padded or fought over; T&M lets work proceed while the cap limits Kestrel's cost risk. The MFA configuration is defined, so a fixed price moves the cost risk to the seller and ties payment to accepted milestones.

check.q: Which vendors in khn_vendors.csv need action on assurance, and what action?
check.a: ClearPath Staffing (V-03) has no report; it runs no Kestrel system and has no remote access, so a security questionnaire and firm contract terms fit the risk. Lumen Analytics Partners (V-05) has a report dated 2025-06-30, more than 12 months old on 2026-10-01; ask for a current report or a bridge letter, and remove its accounts when the contract ends on 2026-11-30.

check.q: Sentinel SOC Services processes Kestrel's security logs in the United States. Is that illegal under Alberta law, and what should Kestrel do?
check.a: No Alberta statute bans it. Section 60 of the Health Information Act requires safeguards for health information stored or used outside Alberta, and Kestrel's own contract requirement keeps data in Canada unless the Chief Privacy Officer approves an exception. Under R-05, Priya Raman reviews it and either removes patient identifiers from forwarded logs, requires Canadian processing, or approves an exception with contract safeguards.

items.summary: You plan how clinicians, agency nurses and vendors move to MFA and single sign-on at shared workstations: an ADKAR-style adoption plan, communication and training by audience, and adoption measures that show whether risk R-03 is under control.

read.heading: Why this change is about people
read.body:
Release 2 asks almost every clinician to sign in differently. Risk R-03 says it plainly: multi-factor authentication (MFA) prompts could slow clinicians at shared workstations. Its owner is Janelle Cardinal (E-008), Director of Patient Flow, because the cost of a slow sign-in lands on patient flow, not on IT.

The starting point in khn_identity.csv on 2026-10-01 is stark:
- 17 of 40 enabled accounts have MFA (42.5%).
- Not one of the enabled registered nurses (10), physicians (5), agency nurses (2) or unit clerks (2) is enrolled.
- Only 4 of 6 privileged accounts have MFA (66.7%).

So MFA is new to nearly every clinician you will ask to change. The technical work is task 15, Roll out MFA and single sign-on, from 2026-10-26 to 2026-11-06 with 4 days of float. The people work has to start well before it. A rollout that is technically perfect but makes nurses share sessions to save time has made Kestrel less safe, not more.

read.heading: ADKAR: five things each person needs
read.body:
ADKAR is a widely used model of individual change: Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, Reinforcement. Each element builds on the one before; skip one and adoption stalls.

| Element | What the clinician needs | Beacon action |
|---|---|---|
| Awareness | Why sign-in is changing | Missed leavers, unprotected admin accounts and the board's ransomware question, told in a two-minute huddle |
| Desire | A reason to want it | Single sign-on means fewer passwords and a badge tap can switch users faster than typing; clinical leaders say so first |
| Knowledge | How to do it | Enrol MFA, tap in and out, what to do when locked out |
| Ability | Doing it under pressure | Practice before go-live, help at the elbow on the first shifts, a fallback that works |
| Reinforcement | Reasons to keep doing it | Show sign-in times, fix complaints fast, retire the old routes |

Use ADKAR to diagnose as well as plan. If enrolment stalls on one unit, ask which element is missing. People who know how but do not want to (Desire) need a different response from people who want to but cannot (Ability). More training fixes Knowledge and nothing else.

read.heading: Know your audiences
read.body:
A charge nurse and a vendor engineer need different messages, so plan by audience:
- Emergency nurses and charge nurses, such as Aisha Mahmoud (E-010) at Kestrel General Hospital (KGH): fast switching at shared workstations, no extra prompts in the middle of care.
- Physicians, such as Dr. Liam O'Connor (E-012) at Aspen Ridge Hospital (ARH), with Dr. Sarah Whitford (E-007) as a visible clinical sponsor.
- Unit clerks, such as Ben Kowalski (E-011) on KGH Medicine 4A, who switch between clerical and bed tasks all shift.
- Agency nurses from ClearPath Staffing (V-03), who may arrive for a first shift with no Kestrel history. Enrolment and awareness training happen on arrival, before the account gives any access to the Clinical Information System.
- Vendor engineers from Meridian Clinical Systems (V-01) and NorthArc Cloud (V-02): MFA on every remote session, no exceptions.
- The service desk, led by Grace Liu (E-005): scripts, knowledge articles and enough staff for the first weeks.

Awareness training completion shows where the effort goes: nursing 86%, physicians 71%, agency and vendor workers 48%, against a 90% target. Physicians and agency staff are the hardest groups to reach, so plan short, flexible sessions rather than a classroom.

read.heading: The communication plan
read.body:
| When | Audience | Message | Channel | Sender |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-10-19 | All clinical staff | Why, what and when | Email and unit huddles | Dr. Helen Marchetti |
| 2026-10-20 | Managers and charge nurses | Your role: start dates, the request form, attestation | 30-minute briefing | Nora Lindqvist and Grace Liu |
| 2026-10-21 | ClearPath, Meridian Clinical Systems (V-01), NorthArc Cloud (V-02) | MFA on every account, end dates, training before access | Contract letter | Daniel Osei (E-004) |
| 2026-10-22 | Service desk | Scripts, knowledge articles, escalation | Briefing | Grace Liu |
| 2026-10-26 to 2026-11-06 | Clinical staff by site | Your enrolment slot and where to get help | Huddles and workstation posters | Super users |
| Weekly from 2026-10-30 | Leaders | Enrolment by site, issues and fixes | Status email | Programme Manager |

These are the dates in Beacon's finished plan; in your own draft, mark them proposed until the sponsor approves.

Four rules make it work. Tell people before it happens to them. Say it more than once, in more than one channel. Use credible messengers: a respected charge nurse beats an IT email. And give people a two-way route, such as a huddle question or a unit champion, so problems come back to you fast.

read.heading: Training and support that fit a shift
read.body:
- Short and role-based: a 10-minute e-learning module completed before enrolment, then an enrolment desk at each site on day and evening shifts from 2026-10-26 to 2026-11-06. That beats an hour in a classroom.
- Super users who help colleagues first: Aisha Mahmoud (E-010) for the KGH emergency department and Ben Kowalski (E-011) for KGH Medicine 4A, one more per site named by the site nurse lead, and super users on night shifts in the first week.
- Practice: let people try enrolling, tapping in and switching users before their go-live.
- Help at the elbow for the first shifts, including nights and weekends, when the service desk is thinnest.
- A fallback: a documented way to sign in when the badge reader or MFA fails, so nobody is tempted to share a session. Shared sessions are the workaround that destroys accountability.
- A firm rule for agency and vendor workers: no account is activated until the worker has enrolled MFA and completed awareness training.
- Knowledge articles for the service desk on enrolment, lockout and lost badges, ready before day one.

Book training against the schedule. The MFA and SSO recommendation pilots badge and PIN sign-in on KGH Medicine 4A inside task 15, before the all-site rollout, so if task 15 starts on 2026-10-26, Medicine 4A needs training the week before, not the week after. Task 19 (2026-11-23 to 2026-11-26) is a different pilot: the Release 2 pilot of the whole access service.

read.heading: Measure adoption, not activity
read.body:
Counting emails sent proves nothing. Measure whether people changed and whether R-03 is under control:

| Measure | Baseline (data) | Target |
|---|---|---|
| Enabled clinical accounts enrolled in MFA | 0 of 19 | 95% by 2026-11-06, 100% by 2026-11-26 (proposed) |
| Privileged accounts with MFA | 66.7% (4 of 6) | 100% (agreed) |
| Awareness training, agency and vendor workers | 48% | 90% (agreed) |
| Access requests through the portal form | 16 of 49 (32.7%) | 90% (proposed) |
| Password-reset tickets | 27 in August and September 2026 | half that rate after single sign-on (proposed) |
| Time to sign in or switch user at a shared workstation | not yet measured; timed on KGH Medicine 4A before the change | no increase (agreed with Janelle Cardinal) |
| Shared or unlocked sessions found in spot checks | none recorded | none (proposed) |

The password-reset count comes from the Password reset category in khn_service_desk.csv, and the portal count from its channel column. The last two measures have no baseline, so take one before go-live, or you will never know whether R-03 got better or worse.

Review the measures weekly with Janelle Cardinal and agree pause criteria in advance. For example: if sign-in time in the Medicine 4A pilot rises above its pre-change baseline (the agreed target is no increase), stop rollout to other units until it is fixed. That turns R-03 from a worry into a managed risk with a trigger and an owner.

keyTerms.definition: A model of individual change with five elements in order: Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability and Reinforcement; a stalled change usually lacks one of them.
What actually changes for a group of people (tasks, tools, timing, skills), used to decide how much communication, training and support each group needs.
A trained member of the unit who helps colleagues first during and after go-live, so frontline questions are answered without waiting for the service desk.
Evidence that people changed how they work, such as MFA enrolment or sign-in time, as opposed to activity measures such as sessions delivered.
Conditions agreed before rollout that trigger stopping further rollout until a problem is fixed, for example sign-in time above an agreed limit.
The person accountable for monitoring a risk and its response; for R-03 it is Janelle Cardinal, because the impact falls on patient flow.

build.goal: Write the Change, communication and training plan that prepares clinicians, agency nurses, vendors and the service desk for MFA and single sign-on, with ADKAR actions, a timed communication plan, training and support, and adoption measures tied to R-03.
steps: In Project, open Change, communication and training plan. Write the change impact for nurses, physicians, unit clerks, agency nurses, vendor engineers and the service desk.
Fill an ADKAR table with at least one concrete action per element, and name a clinical sponsor and super users for each pilot unit.
Build the communication plan with timing tied to task 15 (2026-10-26 to 2026-11-06), audience, message, channel and owner, and mark the dates as proposed.
Write the training and support plan: format, length, practice, help at the elbow, fallback sign-in, service desk knowledge articles, and the activation rule for agency and vendor accounts.

Add the adoption measures with data baselines (0 of 19 clinical accounts with MFA, 66.7%, 48%, 16 of 49 portal requests, 27 password-reset tickets) and targets marked agreed or proposed, and plan how to baseline sign-in time before go-live.
Agree pause criteria for R-03 with Janelle Cardinal and record them in the plan and the RAID log.
Compare with See the finished example, then write Explain it in your own words for the plan.
