Pause rule (proposed): if Medicine 4A's sign-in time is above its baseline when the pilot ends (the agreed target is no increase), rollout to other units stops until it is fixed. The task 19 pilot later tests the whole access service.

examTips.tip: Business Environment task 7, Support organizational change: the best answer is rarely 'send more communication'. Pick the option that supplies what the stakeholder is missing, such as clinical leaders building desire or practice sessions building ability.

People task 8, Plan and manage communication: match channel to audience and purpose. Push channels such as email build awareness; interactive ones such as huddles resolve concerns. Strong answers include a feedback route back to the team.

Organizations and People is the dimension for culture, roles and skills. In rollout scenarios, Progress iteratively with feedback (pilot first) and Collaborate and promote visibility (share adoption measures with the units) are the guiding principles usually tested.

pitfalls: Measuring activity, such as emails sent and sessions held, instead of adoption: MFA enrolment, sign-in time and workarounds found.
Training agency nurses after their first shift. Their accounts should not activate until MFA enrolment and awareness training are done.
Leaving no fallback. When a badge reader fails, clinicians will share sessions unless a safe alternative exists.
Starting communication when task 15 starts. Awareness and desire need lead time, so begin at least a week before, as Beacon's plan does on 2026-10-19.

check.q: A week into the pilot, nurses on one unit know how to enrol but call MFA 'IT's problem' and avoid it. Which ADKAR element is missing, and what do you do?
check.a: Desire is missing; they already have knowledge. Use credible clinical voices: the clinical sponsor and the unit's super users explain what MFA protects and what single sign-on gives back, listen to objections, and fix any workflow pain they raise. More training would not help.

check.q: Why is Janelle Cardinal, not the Chief Information Security Officer, the owner of R-03?
check.a: R-03 is about slower sign-in at shared workstations, and its impact lands on patient flow. The Director of Patient Flow can judge that clinical impact, agree acceptable limits with frontline staff and decide whether to pause rollout. Security still designs MFA; she owns the risk to the workflow.

check.q: Which adoption measures have no baseline yet, and why must you get one before go-live?
check.a: Time to sign in or switch user at a shared workstation, and shared or unlocked sessions found in spot checks. Without a measurement before the change you cannot show whether MFA and single sign-on made R-03 better or worse, and you cannot set fair pause criteria.

items.summary: You take CR-01, a request for a patient-level ALC list on the bed dashboard, through integrated change control: impact on scope, schedule, cost, quality, risk, privacy, security and the service, the change-control board decision of 2026-10-29, the decision record and the baseline updates.

read.heading: Integrated change control in one page
read.body:
Once a baseline is approved, any change to scope, schedule or cost goes through integrated change control. Integrated means you assess the change against everything at once: scope, schedule, cost, quality, risk, privacy, security and the live service. Beacon has one change-control board for the whole programme, chaired by Marcus Bell (E-002), Chief Information Officer.

The seven steps in Beacon's process:
1. Raise: the requester completes the change request form (ID, requester, date, what is asked and why); the Programme Manager logs it within 1 working day.
2. Triage: check it is complete and set the authority level: Programme Manager, board or sponsor.
3. Assess: the data, privacy, security and service leads analyze the impact on every baseline and constraint within 5 working days, for the request as asked and at least one alternative.
4. Decide: the board or the sponsor approves, approves an alternative, defers or rejects, with reasons, and the decision is recorded.
5. Update baselines: each owner updates and re-versions the affected documents.
6. Implement: a live change also needs an IT change record in the IT Service Management Platform (A-011).
7. Verify and close: the requester confirms the result and the log is closed.

Nothing is built before step 4. An analyst who adds 'just a small list' to a live dashboard because a director asked has made an uncontrolled change, however helpful it felt.

read.heading: CR-01: what was asked and why
read.body:
On 2026-10-27, after Release 1 had gone live, Janelle Cardinal (E-008), Director of Patient Flow and business owner of bed data, raised CR-01: a patient-level list of alternate level of care (ALC) patients, with names and bed numbers, on the bed dashboard.

Her reason is real. ALC patients occupy acute beds they no longer need, and the data shows the scale: across the third quarter (Q3, 2026-07-01 to 2026-09-30) there were 2,075 ALC patient-days, 18.4% of occupied bed-days (Kestrel General Hospital (KGH) 835, Aspen Ridge 561, Coulee Valley 377, Prairie Gate 302). She wants to run the daily bed meeting from one screen and see where ALC patients wait. The board met on 2026-10-29.

The request collides with how Release 1 was designed. The dashboards use de-identified, aggregated data and are classified Confidential. Names and bed numbers are individually identifying health information, which Kestrel classifies as Restricted. So the question for the board is not 'is this useful?' but 'what is the least identifying way to meet this need?'

read.heading: Impact analysis across every area
read.body:
| Area | As asked: patient list | Alternative: unit-level counts and days |
|---|---|---|
| Scope | Adds identifying patient detail to a de-identified service, outside the charter | Adds unit-level ALC counts and days, inside the charter |
| Schedule | Not estimated: privacy and architecture rework first; Release 2 gate at risk | 3 days of model work; no change to the Release 2 gate |
| Cost | New work while cost performance is already 0.89 and the forecast exceeds the funding authorized (R-08) | Absorbed in existing analytics effort (agreed); no reserve used |
| Quality | New tests for patient-level accuracy and timeliness | Reconcile ALC days to 2,075 and the site totals; test suppression |
| Risk and privacy | Fails the least-amount and highest-anonymity duties; raises breach impact | Meets them; the R-02 small-count rule applies |
| Security and service | Data becomes Restricted; row-level security by care team; service scope changes | Stays Confidential; small catalogue and knowledge update |

Two impacts need checking, not assuming. Schedule: the work falls to the Clinical Analytics Lead, who has no task on the Release 2 critical path (12 > 14 > 17 > 19 > 20), so 3 days leaves the gate on 2026-11-26 untouched. But R-06 already flags Tomás Rivera (E-006) as a key-person dependency, so confirm his availability; the finished record pairs Mei Tanaka (E-013) with him on the build. Quality and privacy: unit-level counts are small. On 2026-09-30 six of the seven inpatient units had fewer than 5 ALC patients; only KGH Medicine 4A, with 9, had more. Across the quarter, 295 of 643 unit-days had 1 to 4 ALC patients. Kestrel's rule to suppress counts under 5 in reports shared outside the care team therefore applies to the new visual, as it did for Prairie Gate under D-02.

read.heading: The privacy test that decided it
read.body:
The Health Information Act (HIA) sets the test. Section 57 requires a custodian to collect, use or disclose health information with the highest degree of anonymity possible, and to consider first whether aggregate information is adequate. Section 58 requires using only the amount of health information that is essential for the intended purpose.

The purpose here is patient-flow planning: which units carry ALC pressure, and how much. Unit-level counts and days meet that purpose. Names and bed numbers add identity without adding planning value, and the care team already has patient detail in the Clinical Information System (CIS, A-001), where access is role-based and logged.

There is a process consequence too. Under section 64, a custodian must prepare a privacy impact assessment for a new or changed information system that handles individually identifying health information, and submit it to the Information and Privacy Commissioner for review and comment before implementing it. Putting identifying ALC detail into the dashboards would have reopened Beacon's privacy impact assessment. The Commissioner reviews and comments; it does not approve.

read.heading: The decision, the record and the baselines
read.body:
The board's decision on 2026-10-29: not approved as asked. Approved alternative: unit-level ALC counts and days on the bed dashboard, with the care team using the CIS for patient detail. Impact: 3 days of model work, no change to the Release 2 gate.

A decision record makes this defensible later. It holds the change request ID and title; requester and date; the request in their words; the options considered; the impact analysis; the decision and reasons, naming the HIA duties; conditions (counts under 5 suppressed and verified in the row-level security (RLS) test pack before release); who decided and when; and the baselines it changes.

Then update the baselines and documents, each with a new version:
- Requirements and traceability register (BCN-R1-06): the new requirement, its design and its test.
- Date table and DAX (Data Analysis Expressions) catalogue (BCN-R1-20): the new unit-level ALC measures.
- RLS test pack (BCN-R1-21): reconciliation and suppression tests.
- Service catalogue entry and service levels (BCN-R1-23), with a service desk knowledge article.
- RAID (risks, assumptions, issues and decisions) log (BCN-R1-11): the decision, with notes against R-02 and R-06.

Two documents do not change: the classification register (BCN-R1-13) and the privacy impact assessment (BCN-R1-14), because no new data element enters the model. The 3 days are absorbed in existing analytics effort, so the Release 2 gate, the budget at completion and the reserve stay as they are.

Finally, tell Janelle Cardinal yourself, with the alternative and the reason. A 'no' with a better 'yes' attached keeps a key stakeholder on side.

read.heading: Three kinds of change control
read.body:
The same event touches three disciplines, and the exams test the difference:
- Project change control (PMP) protects the baselines. The board decides whether the programme's scope, schedule or cost changes.
- The ITIL change practice protects the live service. The bed dashboard is in production, so releasing the new visual is a change assessed and authorized by the right change authority, logged as an IT change record in the IT Service Management Platform (A-011), scheduled, and communicated so the service desk knows what changed.
- Change management (CISSP, Security Operations) makes sure changes do not weaken security: the classification stays Confidential, row-level security still holds, and the change is tested and documented before release.

On a programme like Beacon one meeting may cover more than one of these, but each question still has to be asked and answered on the record.

keyTerms.definition: Reviewing every change request against all baselines and constraints together, deciding through the change-control board, and updating the baselines only after approval.
The body that approves, rejects or defers changes to the baselines; Beacon has one for the whole programme, chaired by Marcus Bell (E-002).
The written record of a change decision: request, options, impacts, decision, reasons, conditions, decision makers, date and the baselines that change.

keyTerms.term: Highest degree of anonymity and least amount
keyTerms.definition: Health Information Act duties (sections 57 and 58): use the least identifying form of health information possible, consider aggregate data first, and use only the amount essential for the purpose.
A patient occupying a bed who no longer needs the intensity of care that setting provides; Kestrel recorded 2,075 ALC patient-days in Q3.

The ITIL practice that assesses, authorizes and schedules changes to live services so they succeed without harming the service. At Kestrel every live change also needs an IT change record in the IT Service Management Platform (A-011).

build.goal: Update the Change-control process with CR-01 worked through end to end: the logged request, a full impact analysis, the board decision of 2026-10-29, the decision record and every baseline update.
steps: In Project, open Release 1 and the document Change-control process. Check that your process shows all seven steps and who may approve what.
Add CR-01 to the change log: requester Janelle Cardinal (E-008), raised 2026-10-27, the request in her words, and the reason with its data (2,075 ALC patient-days, 18.4% of occupied bed-days in Q3).
Write the impact analysis table for the request as asked and for the alternative, covering scope, schedule, cost, quality, risk, privacy, security and the service.
Name the HIA duties that decide it (sections 57 and 58) and the section 64 consequence of the request as asked.
Write the decision record: decision, reasons, the suppression condition, the chair Marcus Bell (E-002) and the decision date, 2026-10-29.
List each baseline and document that changes, with its new version number, and plan the release to the live dashboard as an authorized change.
Draft your message to Janelle Cardinal, then compare with See the finished example.
build.modelAnswer: CR-01 decision (change-control board, 2026-10-29, chair Marcus Bell): not approved as asked. Reason: names and bed numbers fail the Health Information Act duties of highest degree of anonymity and least amount (sections 57 and 58), and aggregate data meets the planning purpose. Approved alternative: unit-level ALC counts and days on the bed dashboard, counts under 5 suppressed; patient detail stays in the CIS. Impact: 3 days of model work, Release 2 gate unchanged. Updated: requirements and traceability register, DAX catalogue, RLS test pack, service catalogue entry and knowledge article, RAID log; classification register and privacy impact assessment unchanged.

examTips.tip: Business Environment task 3, Manage and control changes: when a stakeholder asks for a change, first log it and assess its impact. Do not implement it, refuse it outright or go straight to the sponsor. The board, not the project manager, approves baseline changes unless authority was delegated.

Domain 1 Security and Risk Management covers legal and regulatory compliance; Domain 7 Security Operations covers change management. A question about adding identifying data to a report usually wants data minimization and a privacy assessment before the change, not a stronger password on the report.

The change practice protects the live service. Releasing a change to a production dashboard needs authorization from the change authority even when a project board has approved the scope. Do not confuse approval of scope with authorization to deploy.

pitfalls: Treating the choice as approve or reject. The strongest outcome is often an alternative that meets the real need inside the rules, as CR-01's unit-level view did.
Analyzing only scope, schedule and cost. CR-01 was decided by privacy, so skipping privacy, security and service impacts misses the point.
Forgetting small counts. Most units have fewer than 5 ALC patients on a given day, so suppression must be built and tested.
Changing the dashboard but not the baselines, the traceability register, the RLS test pack or the service catalogue.

check.q: Why did the board reject the patient-level ALC list but approve unit-level counts?
check.a: The Health Information Act requires the highest degree of anonymity possible and only the essential amount of health information, with aggregate information considered first (sections 57 and 58). Patient-flow planning needs to know which units carry ALC pressure, which counts and days show; names and bed numbers add identity without adding planning value, and the care team already has patient detail in the CIS.

check.q: The alternative needs 3 days of model work. How do you confirm it does not move the Release 2 gate?
check.a: Check who does the work and whether they sit on the Release 2 critical path, 12 > 14 > 17 > 19 > 20. The Clinical Analytics Lead has no Release 2 critical tasks, so the gate on 2026-11-26 holds. Confirm availability anyway, because R-06 flags Tomás Rivera as a key-person dependency.

check.q: Name three documents you update after the decision and one control you must test before release.
check.a: Any three of: the requirements and traceability register, the date table and DAX catalogue, the RLS test pack, the service catalogue entry with its knowledge article, and the RAID log. Before release, test that unit-level ALC counts under 5 are suppressed in views shared outside the care team.

items.summary: You map the access-request value stream across the eight ITIL lifecycle stages, measure where requests wait using the 49 access requests in khn_service_desk.csv, design joiner-mover-leaver events driven by HR from the khn_identity.csv evidence, and write the future-state process.

read.heading: The service and its baseline
read.body:
A value stream is the series of steps an organization takes to create and deliver a product or service to its consumers. Here the service is clinician access, and the outcome the consumer wants is simple: the right access on the first shift, and none after the last. The consumers are new and moving clinicians, agency nurses, vendor engineers and the managers who ask for access. The service owner is Grace Liu (E-005), IT Service Desk Manager.

The baseline from khn_service_desk.csv, August and September 2026:

| Measure | Baseline |
|---|---|
| Access requests logged | 49 |
| Resolved, used for the median | 44 |
| Median time to fulfil | 4.26 days (102.3 hours) |
| Resolved within 72 hours | 27.3% |
| Service level met, recomputed | 15.2% |
| Still open at the extract | 5 |

Splitting the 44 resolved requests by channel (computed from the file) shows where to look: phone requests had a median of 3.47 days (24 requests), walk-up 4.65 days (5) and the portal 5.42 days (15). None of the 14 resolved priority 3 (P3) requests, which carry a 24-hour target, met it; the fastest took 45.8 hours. The portal, the channel meant to be easiest, is the slowest, which suggests requests sit there unseen.

read.heading: Map the stream across the lifecycle stages
read.body:
ITIL Version 5 organizes product and service management into eight lifecycle stages. An access request touches all of them, and a gap in any stage shows up as waiting or risk:

| Stage | What it means for access | Beacon evidence or change |
|---|---|---|
| Discover | Demand and pain: who waits, and what it costs care | 49 requests, 4.26-day median |
| Design | Role catalogue, approval rules, SoD rules, request form | Release 2 role matrix; business owners approve |
| Acquire | What partners supply: tooling, the HR feed, agency and vendor terms | ClearPath end dates, Meridian roster |
| Build | Configured roles, workflows, HR integration, knowledge | Task 14 HR integration |
| Transition | Testing, change approval, training, cut-over | Task 19 pilot and acceptance |
| Operate | Running the directory, HR feed and jobs each day | Identity Directory (A-007) |
| Deliver | Fulfilling each request so access works | Request to working sign-in |
| Support | Help when access fails | Lockouts, resets, incidents |

Cross-check with the four dimensions. Organizations and People: who approves and who provisions, and is anyone doing both? Kevin Park (E-009) is. Information and Technology: the HR and Payroll System (A-015) is the source of truth for employment status and the Identity Directory (A-007) for accounts. Partners and Suppliers: how ClearPath and Meridian tell you about starts and ends. Value Streams and Processes: which steps add value and which only add waiting. SoD here is segregation of duties and HR is human resources.

read.heading: Measure flow: work time, wait time and quality
read.body:
Value stream mapping looks at each step's work time (hands-on effort), its wait time (sitting in a queue) and the share of work that arrives complete and accurate:
- Lead time = total work time + total wait time.
- Flow efficiency = work time / lead time.
- Rolled % complete and accurate = the product of every step's % complete and accurate.

The tickets give you lead time, a median of 102.3 hours, but not work time. You get work time by walking real requests with the people who touch them. In Beacon's finished value stream, a timed walk-through on 2026-11-12 of five requests near the median put the nine steps (ask, log and route, confirm with the manager, approve, check Clinical Information System training, provision, issue credentials, sign in and test, close) at 2.55 hours of hands-on work (estimates). Flow efficiency is 2.55 / 102.3, about 2.5%. The rest is waiting: for an approver who does not know a task is in their queue, for a training record, for an administrator who is also approving.

Quality matters as much as speed. If 7 in 10 requests arrive with everything filled in (70%) and the approval step passes 9 in 10 first time (90%), only 63% get through both steps without rework (illustrative figures). In Beacon's finished map the nine steps multiply to 40.6%, mostly because only about 60% of requests arrive complete (estimates from the walk-through). Every rework loop adds another wait, so fixing the request form can do more than hiring another administrator.

read.heading: Joiner, mover, leaver: drive access from HR events
read.body:
The access stream is really three streams with one source. Human resources (HR), through Nora Lindqvist (E-018) and the HR and Payroll System (A-015), records when someone joins, moves or leaves. Identity should follow those events automatically, not wait for someone to remember a ticket. The data as of 2026-10-01 shows what happens when it does not:
- Leaver missed: E-027 Jason Kim, a registered nurse, was terminated on 2026-08-14; the account is still Enabled 48 days later. The last directory sign-in was 2026-08-13, but the CIS (Clinical Information System) audit log must still be checked for use after termination.
- Contract end missed: E-014 Olivia Grant, an agency nurse from ClearPath, ended her assignment on 2026-08-31; still Enabled 31 days later. Her access review, AR-003, decided Remove on 2026-09-25, and nobody actioned it.
- Mover not cleaned up: E-028 Chantal Roy moved from Unit Clerk on Medicine at Aspen Ridge Hospital to Clinical Analyst at Kestrel General Hospital on 2026-08-17. Her old row was never closed (it should end 2026-08-16), so she still holds Unit Clerk access: A-001 view chart, A-006 update bed status and A-008 virtual desktop access. That is privilege creep.
- No end date: E-015 Raj Patel, a Meridian engineer, has none at all.

One row shows a rule working: E-040 is on leave and the account is Disabled.

read.heading: Design the joiner-mover-leaver workflow
read.body:
| Event | Trigger from HR | Identity action | Timing (proposed) | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Joiner | Hire or assignment record in A-015 | Create account, assign the role from job_role, enrol multi-factor authentication (MFA), check training | Ready before the first shift | Ticket and role assignment logged |
| Mover | Transfer or role change | Add the new role and remove the old role in the same run | On the effective date; any handover overlap only by approved exception, at most 5 working days (proposed) | Old row closed with effective_to |
| Leaver | Termination | Disable the account, remove permissions, end sessions | Same day | Disable time against termination time |
| Contract end | Agency or vendor effective_to | Account expires automatically | On the end date | Expiry set when the account is created |
| Leave | Leave of absence | Disable or suspend; restore on return | Start of leave | As for E-040 |

Design rules:
- Every agency and vendor account gets an end date when it is created (Kestrel rule DQ-12), never later than the contract end.
- A leaver event overrides any open request for that person.
- Movers lose old access by default; keeping it needs an approved, time-bound exception.
- Every event leaves evidence you can count, such as the gap between termination and disable.

These rules drive the measure missed leavers: baseline 2, target 0 (agreed).

read.heading: The future-state process
read.body:
Design the future state by removing waits before adding automation:
1. An HR event or a manager's request creates the ticket; nobody re-keys details.
2. The role's standard access is provisioned without further approval, because the role catalogue was approved once.
3. Extra access is requested from a catalogue item and approved by the system's business owner, never by the administrator who provisions it.
4. Training and MFA enrolment are checked before activation.
5. Provisioning runs from the approved ticket, and the requester and clinician are told when access works.
6. Leavers and contract ends disable access the same day; the HR event opens the ticket automatically, so nobody has to remember to raise one.
7. Every step is timed, so the queue is visible to managers.

The guiding principles keep the design honest: Start where you are (the 4.26-day baseline); Keep it simple and practical (remove approvals that never reject anything); Think and work holistically (joiners, movers and leavers are one stream); and Optimize and automate last, once the steps are simple. The agreed charter targets are a median of 1 day to fulfil and 80% within 72 hours, measured three months after Release 2. The redesign itself is task 17 (2026-11-11 to 2026-11-20), on the critical path, so keep its scope tight.

keyTerms.definition: The series of steps an organization takes to create and deliver a product or service to its consumers, such as a clinician's request through to working access.
Total elapsed time from request to outcome, equal to work time plus wait time; the median access request took 102.3 hours.
Work time divided by lead time; a low figure means most of the lead time is spent waiting in queues rather than being worked on.
The share of work a step receives that it can use without correction; multiplying it across steps shows how much passes first time.
Provisioning, changing and removing access driven by HR events: hire, transfer, termination, contract end and leave.
The build-up of access as people move roles without losing old rights, as E-028 kept Unit Clerk access after becoming a Clinical Analyst.
An Enabled account whose HR status is Terminated or whose effective_to has passed; Kestrel had 2 on 2026-10-01 (E-014, E-027).

build.goal: Produce the Access-request value stream, the Joiner-mover-leaver workflow and the Future-state access process: one baseline, one map across the eight lifecycle stages, HR-driven JML rules backed by data, and a measurable future process.
steps: From Practice, Labs, filter khn_service_desk.csv to Access request and confirm the baseline: 49 logged, 44 resolved, median 4.26 days, 27.3% within 72 hours, 15.2% service level met, 5 still open.

In Project, open Access-request value stream. Fill the eight lifecycle stages and the four dimensions check, then add the nine-step map with work and wait times from walking real requests, labelled as estimates where they come from interviews.
Compute lead time, flow efficiency and rolled % complete and accurate, and name the two biggest waits with the channel evidence (portal 5.42 days against phone 3.47 days).
Open Joiner-mover-leaver workflow. For joiner, mover, leaver, contract end and leave, write the trigger, action, timing, owner and evidence.
Add the evidence cases from khn_identity.csv: E-027, E-014 with AR-003 not actioned, E-028's overlapping rows and old Unit Clerk access, E-015's missing end date, and E-040 as the rule working.
Open Future-state access process. Write the future steps, who approves what, the measures and the agreed targets (median 1 day, 80% within 72 hours, missed leavers 0).
Check all three documents against their Done when checklists, then compare each with See the finished example.
build.modelAnswer: Leaver rule: a termination in the HR and Payroll System (A-015) disables the A-007 account and ends sessions the same day, removes every permission, and logs the gap between termination and disable. Contract end: every Agency and Vendor account is created with effective_to no later than the contract end and expires on that date. Evidence: E-027 terminated 2026-08-14 and E-014 ended 2026-08-31 were both still Enabled on 2026-10-01 (48 and 31 days). Measure: missed leavers, baseline 2, target 0.

examTips.tip: Know the eight Version 5 lifecycle stages in order: Discover, Design, Acquire, Build, Transition, Operate, Deliver, Support. Obtaining an HR feed or agency terms from a partner is Acquire; fulfilling one request is Deliver; helping when access fails is Support.

Optimize and automate comes after simplifying. An answer that automates a tangled approval chain before removing steps is weaker than one that applies Keep it simple and practical and Start where you are first.

Domain 5 Identity and Access Management (IAM), identity and access provisioning lifecycle: the strongest control for missed leavers is an authoritative HR trigger with timely deprovisioning, confirmed by access review. A mover keeping old rights is privilege creep.
Process task 3, Help ensure value-based delivery: measure the outcome the consumer values, such as access ready for the first shift, rather than outputs such as tickets closed.

pitfalls: Mapping only the service desk steps. The waits live in approvals, training checks and HR, so the map must cross teams.
Automating first. Automating today's steps would make a process that is about 2.5% flow-efficient fail faster.
Treating leavers as a separate project. Joiners, movers and leavers come from the same HR events and need one design.
Assuming no sign-in means no harm. E-027's last directory sign-in predates termination, but the CIS audit log must still be checked.

check.q: What does the channel split of resolved access requests suggest, and what would you change?
check.a: Portal requests had a median of 5.42 days against 3.47 for phone, so the channel meant to be easiest waits longest, probably unseen in a queue. Give the portal queue an owner and alerts, route approvals automatically to the business owner, and time each step so waits become visible.

check.q: E-028 moved roles on 2026-08-17. What went wrong, and what rule prevents it?
check.a: The old Unit Clerk row was never closed, so E-028 has two current rows and still holds A-001 view chart, A-006 update bed status and A-008 virtual desktop access from the old job. The mover rule adds the new role and removes the old role's access in the same run on the effective date, allows a handover overlap only through an approved exception, and closes the old row with effective_to 2026-08-16.

check.q: Why is an access request a value stream across all eight lifecycle stages rather than only a Deliver activity?
check.a: Fulfilling one request is Deliver, but its speed and safety depend on Discover (demand), Design (roles and approvals), Acquire (the HR feed and supplier terms), Build (configured workflows), Transition (testing and training), Operate (the directory and feed running daily) and Support (help when access fails). A weak stage shows up as waiting or risk in every request.

items.summary: You compare the designed role permissions in khn_role_permissions.csv with what people actually hold in khn_user_permissions.csv, find the 8 excess grants and Kevin Park's segregation-of-duties conflict, and choose fixes and compensating controls using RBAC, ABAC, least privilege and need to know.

read.heading: Access control models
read.body:
Five models answer the question 'who decides who gets in?':
- Discretionary access control (DAC): the owner of a resource decides. Flexible, hard to govern at scale.
- Mandatory access control (MAC): the system enforces labels and clearances, and users cannot override them.
- Role-based access control (RBAC): permissions attach to roles and people get roles. Easy to review: 'what can a registered nurse do?'
- Attribute-based access control (ABAC): a policy decides using attributes of the user (site, unit, worker type, end date), the resource (classification, owning site), the action and the context (time, workstation). Fine-grained, harder to test and explain.
- Rule-based access control: system-wide rules, such as firewall rules or 'no sign-in outside contract dates'.

Kestrel uses RBAC as the backbone: job_role in khn_identity.csv drives khn_role_permissions.csv. Release 1's row-level security is attribute-based in spirit, because the user's site decides which rows they see. A practical design is RBAC for the coarse grant plus attributes for the limits: an agency nurse gets the Agency Nurse role, but only at the assigned site and only until effective_to. Pure RBAC drifts towards role explosion, a role for every unit and shift; pure ABAC is hard for a manager to review.

read.heading: Least privilege and need to know
read.body:
Least privilege: each person gets the minimum permissions the job needs, for no longer than needed. Need to know: even with the right role, a person sees specific information only when a task requires it. A physician may be able to open charts, but should open only the charts of patients in their care.

In Alberta this is law as well as good practice. Sections 57 and 58 of the Health Information Act (HIA) set the limitation and need-to-know principles: use health information with the highest degree of anonymity possible, and only the amount essential for the purpose. The role-to-permission matrix is how Kestrel shows it applies those duties to its own staff.

Privilege creep is the slow failure of least privilege: people collect rights as they move and never lose the old ones. Access reviews and the mover process exist to stop it, and E-028 shows what happens without them.

read.heading: The designed role-to-permission matrix
read.body:
khn_role_permissions.csv defines 39 permissions across 11 roles. Grouped by system:

| Role | Clinical systems | Access and desktops | Analytics | Other |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Registered Nurse | A-001 view chart, document care; A-002 view tracking board | A-008 virtual desktop access | none | A-013 email |
| Agency Nurse | A-001 view chart, document care | A-008 virtual desktop access | none | none |
| Physician | A-001 view chart, document care, order entry; A-002 view tracking board | A-008 virtual desktop access | A-009 view site dashboards | A-013 email |
| Unit Clerk | A-001 view chart; A-006 update bed status | A-008 virtual desktop access | none | A-013 email |
| Clinical Analyst | none | none | A-009 view site dashboards, build; A-010 query de-identified data | A-013 email |
| Executive | none | A-007 approve access | A-009 view all sites | A-013 email |
| System Administrator | none | A-007 provision accounts; A-008 administer virtual desktops | none | A-013 email |
| Service Desk Analyst | none | A-007 reset passwords | none | A-011 manage tickets; A-013 email |
| Security Analyst | none | A-007 administer audit logs | none | A-011 manage tickets; A-013 email |
| Vendor Support | A-001 remote support | none | none | A-012 remote support |
| Corporate Staff | none | none | none | A-011 submit tickets; A-013 email |

Read it as a design statement. Approving access sits with executives as business owners, provisioning with administrators, and audit-log administration with security: that split is the segregation-of-duties design. Agency nurses get no order entry, and vendors get remote support, not chart viewing.

read.heading: What people actually hold: 8 excess grants
read.body:
khn_user_permissions.csv holds 171 actual grants. An excess grant is a permission that the worker's current role, taken from their latest identity row, does not include. Comparing the two files finds 8:

| Worker | Current role | Excess grant | Granted | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| E-009 Kevin Park | System Administrator | A-007 approve access | 2025-11-03, by himself | Remove; approval belongs to business owners |
| E-009 Kevin Park | System Administrator | A-007 administer audit logs | 2026-02-17, by himself | Remove; belongs to security (E-020) |
| E-013 Mei Tanaka | Clinical Analyst | A-009 view all sites | 2026-08-24, by E-006 | Remove, or approve a time-bound exception |
| E-014 Olivia Grant | Agency Nurse | A-001 order entry | 2026-06-15, by E-009 | Remove, and disable the account |
| E-015 Raj Patel | Vendor Support | A-001 view chart | 2025-06-09, by E-009 | Remove; remote support only |
| E-028 Chantal Roy | Clinical Analyst | A-001 view chart; A-006 update bed status; A-008 virtual desktop access | 2022, in her old Unit Clerk job | Remove all three |

Notice what this comparison cannot catch. E-027, the terminated nurse, holds only registered nurse permissions, so none of them count as excess. Role analysis finds wrong access; only joiner-mover-leaver controls and access reviews find access that should not exist at all.

read.heading: Segregation of duties: the Kevin Park conflict
read.body:
Kestrel's segregation-of-duties (SoD) rule: on the Identity Directory (A-007), no one may hold two or more of provision accounts, approve access and administer audit logs. Someone who can approve and provision can give anyone access with no second pair of eyes. Someone who also administers the audit logs can hide it.

Kevin Park (E-009) holds all three, the only conflict in the data. The surrounding evidence:
- He granted himself approve access (2025-11-03) and administer audit logs (2026-02-17).
- He granted 107 of the 171 permissions in the file, 62.6%.
- He reviewed his own access in the Q3 review (AR-001).
- He is the manager of record for vendor engineer E-015, and the reviewer of that account (AR-002, overdue).

None of this says Kevin did anything wrong. It says nobody could tell if he had, which is issue I-01. The fix: remove approve access and administer audit logs from E-009; give approval to the business owners and audit-log administration to security, Sam Okafor (E-020); re-approve his remaining rights through Daniel Osei (E-004); and redo AR-001 with an independent reviewer.

read.heading: Compensating controls while you fix it
read.body:
Sometimes duties cannot be separated overnight: a small team, a critical system, one person who knows it. Then you add compensating controls, which reduce the same risk another way, and you give them an end date.
- Detective: match every A-007 account or group change to an approved ticket and have Sam Okafor review the weekly match report; an unmatched change is a security incident. Forward A-007 audit events to the security operations centre (SOC), where administrators cannot edit them, once the R-05 privacy review allows it.
- Preventive: require a second approver for any grant on A-007, and route privileged changes through privileged access management with just-in-time elevation.
- Alerting: alert on any change to E-009's own account or rights.
- Administrative: provisioning shared across all three administrators (E-009, E-017, E-033), job rotation and mandatory leave, so someone else regularly does the work and anomalies surface.

Record the arrangement against issue I-01 with a named risk owner, Marcus Bell (E-002), and an end date: the permanent fix in task 16 (Implement privileged access and SoD controls, early finish 2026-11-04). It is not an access exception: Kestrel's exception process never allows anyone to hold two or more of the three A-007 duties. A compensating control is a bridge, not a destination.

keyTerms.definition: Permissions are attached to roles and people receive roles; Kestrel's 11 roles and 39 role permissions are an RBAC design.
A policy grants or denies access using attributes of the user, resource, action and context, such as site, classification or contract end date.
Each person holds only the permissions their job needs, for only as long as they need them.
Access to specific information only when a task requires it, even for someone whose role could reach it; the Health Information Act builds it into sections 57 and 58.
A permission a worker holds that their current role does not include; Kestrel has 8, including E-028's leftover Unit Clerk access.
Splitting sensitive steps so no single person can complete them alone; on A-007 nobody may hold two or more of provision, approve and administer audit logs.
An alternative control that reduces a risk when the primary control cannot be applied yet; it should be independent, owned and time-bound.

examTips.tip: Domain 5 Identity and Access Management (IAM), authorization mechanisms: spot the model from the clue. The owner decides is DAC; labels and clearances is MAC; job function is RBAC; a policy over user, resource and context attributes is ABAC.

Domain 7 Security Operations, foundational security operations concepts: least privilege limits what you can do, need to know limits what information you see, and separation of duties stops one person completing a sensitive task alone. Questions often test them side by side.

Domain 1 Security and Risk Management: a compensating control is the right answer when the primary control cannot be applied now. The best option is independent of the person controlled, owned and time-bound; an acceptance with no end date is weaker.

check.q: Which three permissions make up Kestrel's SoD rule, and why is holding all three worse than holding two?
check.a: Provision accounts, approve access and administer audit logs on A-007. Approve plus provision lets one person grant access unchecked; adding audit-log administration lets them alter the record that would reveal it. Holding all three removes prevention and detection together.

items.summary: You design how Kestrel authenticates people: MFA factors and their strength, single sign-on and federation with SAML and OpenID Connect, fast user switching at shared clinical workstations, break-glass access, and privileged access management to close the 66.7% privileged MFA gap.

read.heading: Authentication factors and what makes MFA strong
read.body:
Identification is who you claim to be (a user ID); authentication proves it; authorization decides what you may do. Authentication factors come in three types:
- Type 1, something you know: a password or personal identification number (PIN).
- Type 2, something you have: a badge, phone app, security key or smart card.
- Type 3, something you are: a fingerprint or face.
Location and behaviour can add context, but are not usually counted as factors on their own.

Multi-factor authentication (MFA) needs two or more different types. A password plus a PIN is still one factor. And not all MFA is equal:
- Codes sent by text message can be intercepted or redirected through SIM (subscriber identity module) swapping.
- Push approvals can be abused through 'MFA fatigue': an attacker floods prompts until someone taps Approve. Number matching, where the user types a number shown on the sign-in screen, reduces it.
- Phishing-resistant methods, such as FIDO2 security keys or passkeys and smart cards, bind the sign-in to the real site, so a fake page cannot replay it.

For biometrics, the false rejection rate (FRR, a Type I error) and false acceptance rate (FAR, a Type II error) trade off against each other. The crossover error rate (CER) is where they are equal; a lower CER means a more accurate system.

read.heading: Kestrel's starting point
read.body:
The data as of 2026-10-01 (khn_identity.csv):
- 40 enabled accounts: 17 with MFA (42.5%), 23 without.
- 6 enabled privileged accounts: E-009 Kevin Park, E-015 Raj Patel (Meridian), E-017 Ahmed Haddad, E-020 Sam Okafor, E-033 Lucas Girard and E-039 Arjun Mehta (NorthArc). Two have no MFA, E-009 and E-015, so privileged MFA coverage is 66.7% against a 100% target (agreed).
- E-031 Noah Bergstrom has privileged recorded as 'Maybe'. Treat it as unknown until the Identity Directory (A-007) is checked and his manager, Grace Liu (E-005), confirms.
- No enabled nurse, physician, agency nurse or unit clerk is enrolled.

The two privileged gaps come first. E-009 holds Kestrel's most dangerous combination of rights. E-015 is a vendor engineer with remote access to the Clinical Information System (CIS, A-001), no MFA and no end date. Close those two before any clinician enrols, and resolve E-031 at the same time.

read.heading: Single sign-on and federation
read.body:
Single sign-on (SSO) lets a person authenticate once and reach many applications. It cuts password fatigue and gives one place to switch access off: disable the account in A-007 and every SSO application closes with it. The trade-off is concentration. If the identity provider is compromised or down, everything is; A-007's recovery time objective (RTO) is 2 hours, and its last restore test passed in 1.5 hours.

Three protocols to know:
- Kerberos: the on-premises workhorse. A key distribution centre issues a ticket-granting ticket at sign-in, then service tickets for each resource. It uses symmetric keys and needs synchronized clocks.
- SAML 2.0 (Security Assertion Markup Language): an identity provider (IdP) sends a signed XML assertion about the user to a service provider (SP), usually through the browser. Common for enterprise web applications.
- OpenID Connect (OIDC): an identity layer on OAuth 2.0 that returns an ID token, a signed JSON Web Token (JWT), describing the authenticated user. Common for modern web and mobile apps. OAuth 2.0 alone is for delegated authorization with access tokens, not for proving who someone is.

Federation extends trust across organizations. Kestrel could accept Meridian's IdP for Meridian engineers: no Kestrel account to create, but Kestrel then trusts Meridian's leaver process and MFA. For privileged vendor access, Kestrel-issued named accounts through privileged access management keep control in Kestrel's hands.

read.heading: Fast user switching at shared clinical workstations
read.body:
Clinicians share workstations and move constantly. A long password plus an MFA prompt every time someone steps up to a keyboard is exactly the delay R-03 warns about. The usual design, described generically:
- At the start of a shift, the clinician taps a badge and enters a PIN: two factors, something you have and something you know.
- For the rest of the shift (up to 12 hours, proposed), a badge tap alone unlocks their own session, or switches to it, within seconds.
- The session lives on the Virtual Desktop Service (A-008), so it follows the clinician: tap at another workstation and the same desktop appears.
- The screen locks after 10 minutes idle (proposed) or when the next person taps in, and a different badge switches user in place. Nobody works in someone else's session.
- Step-up: higher-risk actions, such as remote access or administrator tasks, ask for full MFA again.

The design only passes the R-03 test if the pilot measures it: time to sign in or switch user, and how often sessions are left open. Beacon's proposed target is 10 seconds or less from badge tap to open chart, measured on Medicine 4A at Kestrel General Hospital.

read.heading: Break-glass emergency access
read.body:
Break-glass means planned, controlled emergency access when normal routes fail or a patient's safety depends on speed. There are two kinds.
- Clinical break-glass in the CIS: a clinician opens a chart outside their normal care relationship, for example for a patient transferred in during a resuscitation. The system asks for a reason, grants access, logs it, and someone reviews it afterwards. It keeps need to know intact by making exceptions visible.
- Administrative break-glass: emergency accounts for when the identity system or MFA service is itself down. Keep very few out of daily use (Beacon's design has two A-007 emergency administrator accounts); keep their credentials, such as security keys, sealed in a safe that one person cannot open alone; give them an MFA method that does not depend on the failed service; alert the SOC (security operations centre) the moment one is used; review every use; and issue new credentials afterwards. Beacon also keeps one sealed CIS emergency account per site, held by the nursing supervisor on duty, for when normal sign-in fails.

Test break-glass before you need it. Release 3's downtime plans depend on it working.

read.heading: Privileged access management
read.body:
Privileged access management (PAM) controls administrator rights:
- Separate accounts: an administrator's daily account has no admin rights; a separate privileged account does.
- Vaulting: privileged passwords live in a vault, are checked out per task and rotated after use.
- Just-in-time (JIT) elevation: rights are granted for one task and a time window after approval, then removed. No standing admin rights.
- Phishing-resistant MFA on every elevation.
- Session recording: privileged and vendor sessions are recorded, and their events go to the SOC.
- Review: privileged accounts are reviewed more often than ordinary ones, for example monthly (a proposal), and every one must be justified.

For Kestrel: E-009 and E-015 enrol phishing-resistant MFA now; Meridian and NorthArc sessions are brokered through PAM, approved per session and recorded; E-015 gets an end date no later than the Meridian contract end; and the six privileged accounts move to JIT elevation through task 16.

keyTerms.definition: Authentication using two or more different factor types (know, have, are); two items of the same type, such as a password and a PIN, are still one factor.
Methods such as FIDO2 security keys, passkeys and smart cards that bind the sign-in to the genuine site, so stolen prompts or codes cannot be replayed.
One authentication gives access to many applications, which reduces passwords and means disabling one account removes access everywhere.
Trust between organizations so one party's identity provider vouches for users to another party's services, using protocols such as SAML or OpenID Connect.
SAML passes signed XML assertions from an identity provider to a service provider; OpenID Connect adds an ID token (a JWT) on top of OAuth 2.0 to prove identity.
A planned, controlled emergency route to access, logged, alerted and reviewed after every use.
Granting privileged rights only for an approved task and time window, then removing them, so no one holds standing admin access.

build.goal: Write the MFA and SSO recommendation and the Privileged-account process: factors by user group, the SSO and federation design, fast user switching for shared workstations, break-glass rules and the privileged controls that take privileged MFA from 66.7% to 100%.
steps: In Project, open MFA and SSO recommendation. Record the baseline: 42.5% of enabled accounts and 66.7% of privileged accounts with MFA, the two privileged gaps (E-009, E-015) and the unknown value for E-031.
Choose the factors for each group (clinicians at shared workstations, remote staff, administrators, vendor engineers) and justify each choice against phishing resistance and workflow speed.
Describe the SSO design: which applications use the directory, whether each uses SAML or OIDC, and your decision on federating with Meridian against issuing Kestrel accounts.
Write the shared-workstation design (badge and PIN once per shift, badge tap to unlock or switch, roaming virtual desktop, auto-lock, step-up) and the pilot measures it must pass for R-03.
Open Privileged-account process. Write separate accounts, vaulting, JIT elevation with approval, MFA, session recording, SOC monitoring and review frequency.
Write both break-glass procedures, clinical and administrative, with alerting, review and credential rotation.
List the six privileged accounts with an action and owner for each, then compare both documents with See the finished example.
build.modelAnswer: Privileged accounts on 2026-10-01: E-009, E-015, E-017, E-020, E-033, E-039 (6); E-031 unknown. Without MFA: E-009 and E-015, so coverage is 66.7%. Actions: E-009 and E-015 enrol FIDO2 keys this week; Meridian (E-015) and NorthArc (E-039) sessions brokered through PAM, approved per session and recorded; E-015 given an end date no later than 2029-03-31; all six moved to just-in-time elevation through task 16; E-031 checked in A-007 with Grace Liu. Target: 100% privileged MFA.

examTips.tip: Domain 5 Identity and Access Management (IAM): count factor types, not items. A password plus a security question is single-factor (both something you know); a badge plus a PIN is two-factor.

Domain 5 Identity and Access Management (IAM), federated identity: SAML passes XML assertions from an IdP to an SP; OIDC adds an ID token on OAuth 2.0; OAuth 2.0 alone authorizes, it does not authenticate. To prove identity to a modern web app, OIDC is the answer.

Domain 7 Security Operations, privileged account management: the strongest answers remove standing privilege (just-in-time), separate admin from daily accounts and record sessions. Monitoring alone is weaker than prevention plus monitoring.

pitfalls: Rolling out MFA to clinicians first while two privileged accounts, one of them a vendor's, still have none.
Giving administrators text-message codes. Privileged users need phishing-resistant MFA.
Designing break-glass that depends on the failed system, such as emergency accounts protected by the same MFA service.
Federating with a vendor without contract terms on their leaver process and MFA. Federation moves trust, not risk.

check.q: Why fix E-009 and E-015 before enrolling clinicians, when clinicians are the larger gap?
check.a: Privileged accounts can change access, logs and systems for everyone, so one compromised admin account outweighs many clinician accounts. E-009 holds conflicting rights, and E-015 is a vendor engineer with remote CIS access, no MFA and no end date. Closing those two takes privileged coverage from 66.7% to the agreed 100%.

check.q: How does fast user switching address R-03 without weakening security?
check.a: Badge plus PIN happens once at the start of a shift; after that a badge tap alone brings up the clinician's own roaming virtual desktop, and the idle time-out or the next person's tap locks or switches it. Each person still works only in their own session, high-risk actions step up to full MFA, and the pilot measures sign-in time and open sessions.

check.q: What makes an administrative break-glass account safe to keep?
check.a: It is used only in emergencies and limited in number (two for A-007 in Beacon's design); its credentials are sealed so that one person cannot reach them alone; it uses an MFA method independent of the normal service; any use alerts the SOC; every use is reviewed; and its credentials are changed afterwards. It is tested before an outage.

items.summary: You write user acceptance tests that clinical roles run in the Release 2 pilot, including what must be refused, repair the quarterly access review using the khn_access_reviews.csv evidence (12 of 18 on time, 6 overdue), and design a time-bound access exception process.

read.heading: User acceptance testing for access
read.body:
User acceptance testing (UAT) answers one question: can the people who will use this do their jobs with it, and is everything that should be refused refused? It is not a repeat of technical testing. In Beacon it is task 19, Release 2 pilot and acceptance testing, from 2026-11-23 to 2026-11-26. The schedule names an emergency charge nurse, a unit clerk and the Service Desk Manager; the finished scripts add a physician, a clinical analyst, a vendor engineer and a service desk analyst as testers. It sits on the critical path, so four days is all there is.

Each test script holds a test ID, the requirement it traces to, the role, preconditions, steps, expected result, actual result, pass or fail, evidence and tester. Agree entry criteria (in Beacon: the role-to-permission matrix configured, the human resources (HR) test feed working, badge readers live on the pilot workstations, test accounts created) and exit criteria (every negative, lifecycle and emergency test passes; positive tests pass or have an agreed workaround; no open severity 1 or 2 defect) before the pilot starts, not during it.

Use a test environment with synthetic test patients. Testing access does not need real health information, and the Health Information Act's duty to use only the essential amount of health information applies to testing too.

read.heading: Positive and negative tests by clinical role
read.body:
Positive tests prove access works. Negative tests prove access is refused. For access controls the negative tests matter more, because a missing refusal is invisible in normal use.

| ID | Role and tester | Test | Expected result |
|---|---|---|---|
| UAT-01 | Registered nurse, Aisha Mahmoud (E-010) | Badge and PIN at a shared ED workstation; open a test chart; save a note | Allowed; sign-in time recorded against the proposed 10-second target |
| UAT-05 | Registered nurse, E-010 | Try order entry in the CIS | Refused and logged |
| UAT-06 | Agency nurse test account | Try order entry; try email | Both refused: the Agency Nurse role has neither |
| UAT-07 | Physician, Dr. Liam O'Connor (E-012) | Filter the dashboard to KGH | No KGH rows: row-level security keeps him to ARH |
| UAT-08 | Clinical analyst, Mei Tanaka (E-013) | Open a CIS chart; choose all sites in the Beacon app (A-009) | Both refused: the Clinical Analyst role has no CIS access, and as a Viewer in Site CVH she sees CVH rows only (her "view all sites" grant was removed, SAC-06) |
| UAT-09 | Vendor, Raj Patel (E-015) | Open a chart; start a remote-support session with no approved ticket | Both refused; remote support only in an approved session |
| UAT-10 | Administrator test account | Approve a request; change audit-log settings | Both refused under the SoD rule |
| UAT-13 | HR test feed | A test unit clerk becomes a clinical analyst today | By end of day the old view chart, bed status and virtual desktop access are gone |
| UAT-14 | HR test feed | A test nurse is terminated and an agency test account ends today | Both disabled by end of day; sign-in refused; sessions ended |

Here ED is emergency department, PIN personal identification number, CIS the Clinical Information System (A-001), KGH Kestrel General Hospital, ARH Aspen Ridge Hospital and SoD segregation of duties. The IDs match the finished test scripts, which also hold positive tests for the unit clerk, physician and analyst (UAT-02 to UAT-04), a self-approval test (UAT-11), a joiner test (UAT-12), a self-review test (UAT-15) and two emergency-access tests (UAT-16 and UAT-17). Each negative test traces to a real finding: E-014's order entry, E-028's old access, E-027's missed termination and E-009's conflict.

read.heading: Defects, evidence and sign-off
read.body:
Log every failure as a defect with a severity, an owner and a retest date. A failed negative test, meaning access was allowed that should have been refused, is a security defect (severity 1 in Beacon's scripts) and blocks sign-off however many positive tests pass.

Keep evidence a reviewer can check later: screenshots of refusals, directory change records with timestamps, ticket IDs, and the tester's name and date. 'Worked for me' is not evidence.

Business owners sign off for their areas: in Beacon, Dr. Sarah Whitford (E-007) for emergency roles, Janelle Cardinal (E-008) for unit roles and sign-in time (R-03), Daniel Osei (E-004) for security tests and Grace Liu (E-005) for service desk tests. That sign-off is formal acceptance of the deliverable, which the PMP calls validating scope. Checking that each script ran and passed is quality control, and the test team does it before sign-off. Keep the two apart: the testers prove it works; the owners decide it is acceptable.

read.heading: The Q3 access review: results
read.body:
An access review, also called recertification, asks each manager or system owner to confirm that each person's access is still needed: keep, modify or remove. khn_access_reviews.csv holds Kestrel's third-quarter (Q3) campaign. As of 2026-10-01:
- 24 review items: 18 were due by 2026-09-30 and 6 are not yet due (due 2026-10-15).
- 12 of the 18 due items were completed on time: 66.7%, against a 100% target (agreed).
- 6 are overdue: AR-002, AR-004, AR-006, AR-012, AR-014 and AR-016. Escalate each to the reviewer's manager.
- Across all 24 items, 14 have a valid decision (58.3%): Keep 11, Modify 1, Remove 2.
- One item is kept under an exception: AR-010.

The overdue list is not random. AR-004 is the review of E-027, the missed leaver, so the control that should have caught the termination has not run. AR-002 is the review of vendor engineer E-015, assigned to Kevin Park (E-009), who manages that account and holds the SoD conflict.

read.heading: What the review data says about the process
read.body:
Four records show how a review can look complete and still fail:
- AR-001: Kevin Park reviewed his own access. Not independent; re-review by Daniel Osei (E-004).
- AR-006: completed on 2026-08-28, before it was assigned on 2026-09-01. Not valid evidence, so treat it as not done and repeat it. It is the review of E-028, the mover whose old access was never removed.
- AR-018: a review for E-045, who is not in khn_identity.csv. An account exists in the CIS for someone HR does not know. The Remove decision is right; confirm the account is gone and find out how it was created.
- AR-003: the reviewer decided Remove for E-014 on 2026-09-25, and the account is still Enabled. A decision nobody carries out is not a control.

Design rules for the workflow:
1. Build the review population from the directory and reconcile it to HR.
2. Assign reviewers by rule and block self-review.
3. Take timestamps from the system, never from the reviewer.
4. Send reminders before the due date and escalate on it.
5. Require a reason for Keep on privileged and vendor accounts.
6. Turn every Remove into a ticket with a deadline, and verify it.
7. Report completion of due items, overdue items and removals actioned.

read.heading: The access exception process
read.body:
Sometimes a person needs access their role does not give, or a control cannot apply yet. An exception makes that visible, bounded and owned instead of quiet:
1. Request: who, which access, why, and for how long (at most 90 days in Beacon, proposed).
2. Assess: the risk, and the compensating controls that reduce it.
3. Approve: the system's business owner approves as the named risk owner; privileged exceptions also need the Chief Information Security Officer, Daniel Osei (E-004), to countersign.
4. Record: in an exception register with an expiry date. No open-ended exceptions.
5. Monitor: alerts or extra review while the exception lasts.
6. Expire or renew: on the expiry date the access goes, unless a fresh approval exists.

Kestrel's data has one exception today, AR-010: E-039 Arjun Mehta of NorthArc Cloud keeps remote support access to the Backup Platform (A-012). The file records only 'Y': no reason, expiry, compensating control or risk owner, which is exactly what the process fixes. Beacon registers it as EX-001, with Marcus Bell (E-002), the Backup Platform's business owner, as risk owner and an end no later than 2026-11-30 (proposed).

Some access can never be an exception: a privileged account without multi-factor authentication (MFA), approving or reviewing your own access, holding two or more of the three A-007 duties, access with no current HR record or after the end date, and shared accounts other than sealed break-glass accounts. So Kevin Park's conflict is removed in task 16, not excepted; its interim compensating controls sit against issue I-01.

keyTerms.definition: Testing by the people who will use the system, against agreed acceptance criteria, ending in formal sign-off by the business owners.
A test that proves the system refuses what it should, such as an agency nurse being denied order entry; a failure is a security defect.
Conditions agreed in advance for starting testing (environment and accounts ready) and for finishing it (critical tests passed, no severe defects, sign-off).
A periodic check in which managers or owners confirm each person's access is still needed and decide to keep, modify or remove it.
Valid on-time review decisions divided by items due; Kestrel's Q3 figure is 12 of 18, or 66.7%.
Approved access outside the standard role, recorded with a reason, compensating controls, a risk owner and an expiry date.

build.goal: Write the User-acceptance test scripts, the Quarterly access-review workflow and the Access exception process, so the pilot proves access works and is refused where it should be, reviews become timely and valid, and exceptions are time-bound and owned.
steps: In Project, open User-acceptance test scripts. Write the entry and exit criteria and the script format, then at least nine scripts covering each pilot role, at least half of them negative tests traced to a data finding.
Plan the four pilot days (2026-11-23 to 2026-11-26): who tests what, the test environment with synthetic patients, defect handling and who signs off.
From Practice, Labs, open khn_access_reviews.csv and confirm: 18 due, 12 on time (66.7%), 6 overdue, 6 not yet due, 14 valid decisions of 24.
Open Quarterly access-review workflow. Record the four process failures (AR-001, AR-006, AR-018, AR-003) and write the design rule that prevents each.
Write the review cycle: population, reviewer rules, reminders and escalation, reasons for Keep, actioning removals, and the measures you will report.
Open Access exception process. Write the six steps, the register fields, the expiry rule and the list of what can never be an exception, then enter AR-010 as the first case, EX-001.
Compare each document with See the finished example, then answer Check yourself for each.
build.modelAnswer: UAT-06 (negative). Requirement: agency nurses view charts and document care but cannot order or use email (role-to-permission matrix). Role: Agency Nurse test account, CIS test environment, test patient. Steps: tap in, open the test chart, select order entry and try to place a laboratory order; then try to open email. Expected: both refused, and the attempts logged. Evidence: screenshot plus the log entry ID. Traces to E-014, who held order entry outside her role. Pass needed for sign-off; a failure is a severity 1 security defect.

examTips.tip: Process task 2, Develop and manage project scope, and Process task 7, Plan and optimize quality of products/deliverables: quality control checks that tests pass; validating scope is the customer's formal acceptance. Business owners, not the test team, accept the pilot results.

Domain 6 Security Assessment and Testing: collecting security process data includes account management and management review. Access review questions reward independence (no self-review), a complete population reconciled to HR, and verified follow-through on removals.

Domain 6 Security Assessment and Testing: negative testing (misuse cases) checks that a system refuses what it should. For access control, one failed negative test is a security defect even if every positive test passes.
Testing, training and cut-over belong to the Transition stage of the lifecycle. If a question asks where acceptance testing of a new access service sits, the answer is Transition.

pitfalls: Writing only positive tests. Most Release 2 findings (E-014's order entry, E-028's old access, E-009's self-approval) are failures to refuse.
Counting a review as done because a date is filled in. AR-006 was 'completed' before it was assigned.
Leaving Remove decisions to chance. AR-003 decided Remove and E-014 stayed Enabled.
Exceptions with no expiry. AR-010 has no end date, so it would never come back for review.

check.q: What makes AR-006 invalid, and why does it matter beyond one record?
check.a: It was completed on 2026-08-28, before it was assigned on 2026-09-01, so it cannot be genuine evidence of a review. It also covers E-028, whose old Unit Clerk access was never removed, so the invalid Keep let privilege creep stand. The workflow should take timestamps from the system and block completion before assignment.

check.q: Write one negative UAT test that traces to a finding in the data.

items.summary: You build the access-governance dashboard in Power BI: a small identity model from the Kestrel files, eight DAX measures that reproduce the approved figures, an accessible page for security and privacy leaders, and the security, refresh and alert settings a Confidential report needs.

read.heading: Who the dashboard is for and what it must show
read.body:
The access-governance dashboard is how leaders see whether Release 2 is working. Its audience is small: Daniel Osei (E-004, Chief Information Security Officer), who owns it and approves every measure definition; Marcus Bell (E-002, Chief Information Officer); Grace Liu (E-005, service owner); Priya Raman (E-003, Chief Privacy Officer); Nora Lindqvist (E-018, human resources); Sam Okafor (E-020, security analyst); and the identity and access team, who use it every week. Tomás Rivera (E-006) builds it. Its deliverable summary names eight things, each a Data Analysis Expressions (DAX) measure: enabled and disabled accounts, missed leavers, privileged accounts, multi-factor authentication (MFA) gaps, review completion, overdue reviews, duty conflicts and request time.

The data is about staff, not patients. Staff records are personal information under the Protection of Privacy Act (POPA), not health information under the Health Information Act, and Kestrel's data dictionary classifies the identity fields as Confidential. So the report carries a Confidential sensitivity label and goes only to the people above.

read.heading: The model behind it
read.body:
Import four files in Import mode, keep each query's name, and fix one thing in Power Query first. khn_identity.csv has 43 rows for 42 workers because E-028 has two current rows, so keep the latest row per worker (SourceFolder is a text parameter holding your folder path):

```
let
    Source = Csv.Document(
        File.Contents(SourceFolder & "khn_identity.csv"),
        [Delimiter = ",", Encoding = 65001, QuoteStyle = QuoteStyle.Csv]
    ),
    Promoted = Table.PromoteHeaders(Source, [PromoteAllScalars = true]),
    Typed = Table.TransformColumnTypes(
        Promoted,
        {{"effective_from", type date}, {"effective_to", type date}}
    ),
    Sorted = Table.Buffer(
        Table.Sort(Typed, {{"employee_id", Order.Ascending}, {"effective_from", Order.Descending}})
    ),
    CurrentRow = Table.Distinct(Sorted, {"employee_id"})
in
    CurrentRow
```

Table.Buffer fixes the sorted order so Table.Distinct keeps the newest row. Then relate khn_identity[employee_id] one-to-many, single direction, to khn_user_permissions (171 rows) and khn_access_reviews (24 rows). Leave khn_role_permissions unrelated. Reuse the cleaned FactServiceTicket query from Release 1 for request time. AR-018's employee, E-045, has no identity row, so it relates to the blank row and stays visible as an unknown worker.

read.heading: Measures 1 to 4: accounts, leavers, privilege and MFA
read.body:
Every measure uses the as-of date 2026-10-01. Adding + 0 shows a zero as 0 instead of blank, which matters for zero-target counts.

```
Accounts =
COUNTROWS ( khn_identity )

Missed Leavers =
VAR AsOf = DATE ( 2026, 10, 1 )
RETURN
    COUNTROWS (
        FILTER (
            khn_identity,
            khn_identity[account_status] = "Enabled"
                && (
                    khn_identity[hr_status] = "Terminated"
                        || (
                            NOT ISBLANK ( khn_identity[effective_to] )
                                && khn_identity[effective_to] < AsOf
                        )
                )
        )
    ) + 0

Privileged Accounts =
CALCULATE (
    [Accounts],
    khn_identity[account_status] = "Enabled",
    khn_identity[privileged] = "Yes"
)

Privileged Without MFA =
CALCULATE ( [Privileged Accounts], khn_identity[mfa_enrolled] = "No" ) + 0

Privileged MFA % =
DIVIDE ( [Privileged Accounts] - [Privileged Without MFA], [Privileged Accounts] )
```

Put account_status beside [Accounts] to show Enabled 40 and Disabled 2. Testing for "Yes" exactly means E-031's 'Maybe' is not counted as privileged; show it on a data-quality card.

read.heading: Measures 5 to 8: reviews, conflicts and request time
read.body:
```
Reviews Due =
VAR AsOf = DATE ( 2026, 10, 1 )
RETURN
    COUNTROWS ( FILTER ( khn_access_reviews, khn_access_reviews[due_date] < AsOf ) )

Review Completion % =
VAR AsOf = DATE ( 2026, 10, 1 )
VAR OnTime =
    COUNTROWS (
        FILTER (
            khn_access_reviews,
            khn_access_reviews[due_date] < AsOf
                && NOT ISBLANK ( khn_access_reviews[completed_date] )
                && khn_access_reviews[completed_date] >= khn_access_reviews[assigned_date]
                && khn_access_reviews[completed_date] <= khn_access_reviews[due_date]
        )
    )
RETURN
    DIVIDE ( OnTime, [Reviews Due] )

Overdue Reviews =
VAR AsOf = DATE ( 2026, 10, 1 )
RETURN
    COUNTROWS (
        FILTER (
            khn_access_reviews,
            khn_access_reviews[due_date] < AsOf
                && (
                    ISBLANK ( khn_access_reviews[completed_date] )
                        || khn_access_reviews[completed_date] < khn_access_reviews[assigned_date]
                )
        )
    ) + 0

SoD Conflicts =
VAR PerWorker =
    ADDCOLUMNS (
        VALUES ( khn_user_permissions[employee_id] ),
        "@ConflictRights",
            CALCULATE (
                DISTINCTCOUNT ( khn_user_permissions[permission] ),
                khn_user_permissions[system_id] = "A-007",
                khn_user_permissions[permission]
                    IN { "provision accounts", "approve access", "administer audit logs" }
            )
    )
RETURN
    COUNTROWS ( FILTER ( PerWorker, [@ConflictRights] >= 2 ) ) + 0

Access Requests Within 72h % =
VAR Resolved =
    FILTER (
        FactServiceTicket,
        FactServiceTicket[TicketType] = "Access request"
            && NOT ISBLANK ( FactServiceTicket[ResolutionHours] )
    )
RETURN
    DIVIDE (
        COUNTROWS ( FILTER ( Resolved, FactServiceTicket[ResolutionHours] <= 72 ) ),
        COUNTROWS ( Resolved )
    )
```

Measure 8 is the Release 1 measure [Median Access Request Days], shown with Access Requests Within 72h %. SoD is segregation of duties.

read.heading: Reconcile, then design the page
read.body:
| # | Measure | Expected on 2026-10-01 | Target |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Accounts by account_status | Enabled 40, Disabled 2 | not applicable |
| 2 | Missed Leavers | 2 (E-014, E-027) | 0 (agreed) |
| 3 | Privileged Accounts | 6 | each justified (proposed) |
| 4 | Privileged Without MFA; Privileged MFA % | 2; 66.7% | 0; 100% (agreed) |
| 5 | Review Completion % | 66.7% (12 of 18) | 100% (agreed) |
| 6 | Overdue Reviews | 6 | 0 (proposed) |
| 7 | SoD Conflicts | 1 (E-009) | 0 (proposed) |
| 8 | Median Access Request Days; Within 72h % | 4.26; 27.3% | 1; 80% (agreed) |

Slice tests help too: by worker_type, Privileged Accounts shows Employee 4 and Vendor 2, and Missed Leavers shows Agency 1 and Employee 1. If a figure differs, find the rule you applied differently before you touch the measure. The usual cause is skipping the current-row step: Accounts then shows 43.

Page design: eight cards in one row in this order, each showing its target and a text status, On target or Off target, so status never depends on colour alone; conditional formatting can add colour as a second signal. Below, an action table listing the employee or review IDs behind each off-target card, with no names and no health information. Add drillthrough from any worker to their permissions and review items, and a visual of overdue items by reviewer. Give every visual alt text, set a logical tab order, and use Performance Analyzer to check the measures that iterate tables.

read.heading: Secure and distribute it
read.body:
- Workspace: a separate workspace, Beacon Access Governance. Viewer for the access-governance group; Member only for the builder, Tomás Rivera, and his backup, Mei Tanaka (E-013). Row-level security (RLS) restricts only Viewers, so anyone with an edit role sees every row.
- RLS: none is needed today, because every viewer may see every row. If managers later get a view of only their own team's review items, add a role that filters to their team and test it with View as.
- Sensitivity label: Confidential on the model and report, so exported files carry the label.
- Refresh: daily at 06:30 (proposed). The identity extracts come from the Identity Directory (A-007), which runs on premises, so scheduled refresh goes through the on-premises data gateway. It went live on 2026-11-13, after the firewall change recorded in the team charter and conflict record (BCN-R2-16).
- Alerts: pin the Missed Leavers card to a dashboard; Daniel Osei and Grace Liu each set a data alert on that tile for any value above 0. Classic Power BI data alerts are set in the Power BI service, not in Desktop, on dashboard tiles that are cards, gauges or key performance indicator (KPI) visuals, and each one is personal: it notifies only the person who set it. To alert directly on a report visual, Fabric Activator alerts are the tool.
- Ownership: Daniel Osei owns the content and approves measure changes. With Mei Tanaka as backup, the model does not add to the key-person dependency on Tomás Rivera (R-06).

keyTerms.definition: For effective-dated identity data, keep only each worker's latest row before measuring; otherwise E-028's two rows inflate Accounts to 43.
Enabled accounts whose hr_status is Terminated or whose effective_to is before 2026-10-01; the result is 2 (E-014, E-027).
Valid on-time review decisions divided by review items due by the as-of date; completed_date must be on or after assigned_date. Kestrel's result is 66.7%.
CALCULATE inside a row iterator such as ADDCOLUMNS turns the current row into a filter, which is how SoD Conflicts counts permissions per worker.
A Microsoft Purview label applied in Power BI, such as Confidential, that travels with exported content and signals handling rules.

A personal notification set in the Power BI service on a dashboard tile (card, gauge or KPI) when its value crosses a threshold, such as Missed Leavers above 0; only the person who set it is notified. Fabric Activator alerts can watch report visuals instead.

build.goal: Build the Access-governance dashboard: an identity model from the Kestrel files, the eight measures in DAX reconciled to the approved figures, an accessible page for security and privacy leaders, and its security, refresh and alert settings.

Create the relationships from khn_identity[employee_id] to the permission and review tables, add the cleaned FactServiceTicket query from Release 1, and check that AR-018 shows against a blank worker.

Build the page: eight cards with targets and conditional formatting, the action table, drillthrough to a worker page, overdue items by reviewer, and alt text on every visual.

Review Completion % 66.7%, 12 of 18 (target 100%). Overdue Reviews 6 (target 0). SoD Conflicts 1, E-009 (target 0). Median Access Request Days 4.26, within 72 hours 27.3% (targets 1 day and 80%). examTips.tip: Manage and secure Power BI: RLS restricts only users with the Viewer role or app access. Admins, Members and Contributors see all rows. If a Member sees data RLS should hide, change their workspace role rather than the RLS filter.
Model the data: COUNTROWS over an empty FILTER returns blank, not zero, so add + 0 when a card must show 0. Use DIVIDE for ratios so a zero denominator returns blank instead of an error.

Classic data alerts are set in the Power BI service on dashboard tiles (cards, gauges, KPIs) and are personal to the user who sets them. A requirement to be notified when missed leavers rise above 0 means pin the card to a dashboard and set an alert; to alert directly on a report visual, use Fabric Activator.

Domain 6 Security Assessment and Testing: key performance and risk indicators are security process data. A good access indicator has a definition, a source, a target and an owner, like Privileged MFA % at 66.7% against 100%.

pitfalls: Skipping the current-row step: E-028's two rows make Accounts 43 and Enabled 41.
Treating 'Maybe' as Yes. Count privileged = "Yes" only and show E-031 as a data-quality item.
Counting AR-006 as complete. A review completed before it was assigned is overdue, which is why the measures compare completed_date with assigned_date.
Publishing where leaders hold Member roles. RLS will not restrict them, and edit rights on a Confidential report belong with the builders.

check.q: Why does Overdue Reviews return 6 and not 5, when only 5 due items have a blank completed_date?
check.a: AR-006 has a completed_date of 2026-08-28, earlier than its assigned_date of 2026-09-01, so it is not valid evidence. The measure treats a blank completed_date or one before assignment as not done, so AR-002, AR-004, AR-012, AR-014 and AR-016 plus AR-006 give 6.

check.q: How does the SoD Conflicts measure find Kevin Park and nobody else?
check.a: It builds a table of each employee_id in khn_user_permissions, uses CALCULATE to count the distinct conflicting permissions each holds on A-007, and counts workers with 2 or more. Executives hold only approve access, E-017 and E-033 only provision accounts and E-020 only administer audit logs, so only E-009, with all three, is counted.

check.q: Suppose the Chief Information Officer (CIO) were a Member of the access-governance workspace and a new RLS role limited managers to their teams. What would the CIO see, and is that right?
check.a: The CIO sees every row, because RLS applies only to Viewers and app users. Seeing everything may suit a CIO, but Member also grants edit rights; if the CIO only needs to read, give Viewer or app access so edit rights stay with the builders.
